title: Balanced Aerial Defence Starting Position
primarySkill: Establishing a balanced defensive starting position before an aerial contest.
objective: Develop a repeatable starting position that allows defenders to see the football, monitor their opponent and move efficiently into an aerial contest.
groundSize: One 10 x 8-metre channel for each group of three players.
coachingDifficulty: 2 – Basic coaching knowledge with one main teaching point
setup:
Mark a starting cone for the defender in the centre of each channel.
Position an attacker approximately 2 metres goal side of the defender.
Position a feeder 8–10 metres in front of the pair with a football.
The defender begins close enough to influence the attacker but without making contact.
The feeder uses hand signals or ball movement to direct the defender’s adjustment.
Create enough channels to keep waiting time minimal.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacker stands still while the defender establishes a balanced starting position.
The defender positions slightly goal side, with knees flexed, weight through the middle of the feet and body opened sufficiently to see both the attacker and feeder.
The feeder moves the football from side to side or takes one or two steps laterally.
The defender adjusts with short, controlled steps while maintaining vision of both the football and opponent.
On the feeder’s call, the attacker moves one or two steps in any direction.
The defender mirrors the movement without crossing the feet or losing goal-side position.
No kick is delivered during the introductory repetitions.
Players rotate through defender, attacker and feeder roles after four to six repetitions.
coachingPoints: Begin close enough to influence the attacker without standing directly behind them.
Keep the feet approximately shoulder-width apart and avoid locking the knees.
Maintain a low, balanced position that permits movement in every direction.
Use peripheral vision rather than repeatedly turning the head away from the football.
Position slightly goal side unless the tactical situation requires otherwise.
Make small adjustment steps instead of leaning or reaching.
Keep the chest open to the football while maintaining awareness of the opponent.
Communicate early when working with another defender or goalkeeper.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the defender can see both the feeder and attacker before movement begins.
Whether the defender remains balanced rather than standing upright or flat-footed.
Whether the defender adjusts with short steps.
Whether goal-side position is preserved when the attacker moves.
Whether the defender turns completely towards the opponent and loses sight of the football.
Whether players understand the difference between close checking and illegal holding.

commonErrors.error: Defender stands directly behind the attacker.
commonErrors.correction: Move half a step to the side and open the body towards the football.

commonErrors.error: Defender stands upright with weight on the heels.
commonErrors.correction: Lower the hips, soften the knees and place weight through the middle of the feet.

commonErrors.error: Defender watches only the attacker.
commonErrors.correction: Use peripheral vision and maintain an open chest towards the feeder.

commonErrors.error: Defender watches only the football and loses the opponent.
commonErrors.correction: Check the opponent’s position through body contact awareness and peripheral vision.

commonErrors.error: Defender crosses the feet when adjusting.
commonErrors.correction: Use short shuffle and drop steps to maintain balance.

commonErrors.error: Defender begins too far away to influence the contest.
commonErrors.correction: Reduce the starting separation to approximately an arm’s length.

progressions: Allow the attacker to make longer leads within the channel.
Have the feeder deliver a gentle lob for the defender to track without contesting.
Add a second attacker so the defender must scan and identify the most dangerous player.
Introduce a second defender and require communication about responsibility.
Vary the defender’s starting position according to field location.
regressions: Keep the attacker stationary while the defender practises the stance.
Use visual floor markers to show the correct goal-side position.
Slow the attacker’s movement to walking pace.
Allow the defender to reset fully between each movement.
Remove the football and use the feeder’s pointing direction as the movement cue.
successIndicators: Establish a balanced stance before the attacker moves.
Maintain vision of both the football and opponent.
Preserve goal-side positioning during short movements.
Adjust without crossing their feet or losing balance.
Remain close enough to influence the eventual aerial contest.
matchApplication: The drill establishes the starting position required when defending a leading forward, resting midfielder or opponent positioned inside 50. A defender who can see both the football carrier and opponent is better prepared to judge the kick, close space, initiate legal bodywork and contest the football in the air.

title: Goal-Side Body Alignment
primarySkill: Maintaining goal-side body alignment against a moving opponent.
objective: Teach defenders to remain goal side while using efficient hip and shoulder alignment to respond to an attacker’s lead.
groundSize: 12 x 10-metre channels.
coachingDifficulty: 2 – Basic coaching knowledge with one main teaching point
setup:
Set two gates 6 metres apart at the attacking end of each channel.
Place the attacker and defender together at a central starting cone.
The feeder stands 10–12 metres away with a football.
The defender begins slightly goal side and half a step to one side of the attacker.
The attacker may lead towards either gate.
The feeder initially holds the football and does not kick.
howTheDrillWorks:
On the feeder’s signal, the attacker leads towards either gate.
The defender reacts while attempting to remain between the attacker and the scoring end.
The defender uses a hip turn, drop step or controlled crossover only after the initial movement has been identified.
The defender closes towards the attacker’s line without cutting across the attacker’s legs.
The repetition ends when the attacker passes through a gate or the defender reaches a balanced contesting position beside the attacker.
The feeder provides a second movement cue before selected repetitions to test the defender’s ability to redirect.
After four repetitions, the attacker and defender change roles.
Feeders rotate after each pair has completed both roles.
coachingPoints: Begin slightly goal side rather than square and level with the attacker.
Turn the hips towards the anticipated lead while keeping the shoulders sufficiently open to the football.
Use the first three steps to protect the dangerous space.
Avoid chasing directly behind the attacker.
Close to the attacker’s inside shoulder without making early illegal contact.
Maintain balance so a change of direction can be answered.
Accelerate only after reading the attacker’s initial movement.
Use the boundary or support defenders when deciding which space to concede.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the defender begins in a genuine goal-side position.
Whether the first step protects dangerous space.
Whether the defender opens the hips efficiently.
Whether the defender runs behind the attacker rather than alongside.
Whether the defender remains balanced when the attacker changes direction.
Whether the defender’s closing line creates a legal contesting position.

commonErrors.error: Defender starts level with the attacker.
commonErrors.correction: Move half a step goal side before the repetition begins.

commonErrors.error: Defender turns completely away from the football.
commonErrors.correction: Open the hips while keeping the head and near shoulder connected to the feeder.

commonErrors.error: Defender chases directly behind.
commonErrors.correction: Run to the attacker’s inside shoulder and protect the scoring side.

commonErrors.error: Defender guesses and moves before the attacker.
commonErrors.correction: Hold a balanced stance until the lead direction is identified.

commonErrors.error: Defender cuts across the attacker’s legs.
commonErrors.correction: Close beside the opponent rather than through their running line.

commonErrors.error: Defender overcommits and cannot redirect.
commonErrors.correction: Shorten the first steps and keep the hips underneath the body.

progressions: Allow the feeder to kick to the attacker after the defender establishes position.
Permit the attacker to use a double lead.
Add a second feeder to change the direction of the incoming football.
Create a scoring system based on the defender arriving goal side and within spoiling distance.
Add a supporting defender who communicates which lead should be covered.
regressions: Restrict the attacker to one nominated gate.
Have the attacker move at three-quarter pace.
Mark the defender’s preferred running line with flat markers.
Pause after the first step and correct body alignment before continuing.
successIndicators: Start goal side of the attacker.
Protect the most dangerous lead corridor.
Turn and accelerate without losing balance.
Arrive in a position from which the football can be legally contested.
matchApplication: The drill reflects the defender’s responsibility when an opponent leads towards goal. Effective goal-side alignment reduces the attacker’s access to dangerous space and gives the defender a better opportunity to spoil, intercept or force the kick towards the boundary.
relatedDrills: SP-001 – Balanced Aerial Defence Starting Position

title: Controlled Aerial Approach
primarySkill: Approaching an aerial contest under control.
objective: Develop the defender’s ability to close space quickly before reducing speed and arriving balanced at the aerial contest.
groundSize: 15 x 8-metre channels.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations or several behaviours
setup:
Place an attacker at the far end of each channel.
Position a defender 4–6 metres goal side of the attacker.
Place a feeder 12–15 metres in front of the attacker.
Mark a 3-metre contest zone around the attacker.
The attacker remains stationary during the first phase.
The feeder delivers controlled, looping kicks into the contest zone.
howTheDrillWorks:
The feeder signals before delivering a high, controlled kick towards the attacker.
The defender accelerates to close the initial space.
As the football begins to descend, the defender shortens the stride and enters the contest zone under control.
The defender reaches a balanced position beside or slightly behind the attacker.
During early repetitions, the defender does not spoil and instead calls “set” when a safe contesting position has been reached.
The attacker catches the football uncontested.
The defender then exits the contest zone and resets.
Players rotate after four kicks in each role.
coachingPoints: Read the football’s flight immediately after it leaves the feeder’s boot.
Accelerate through open space rather than approaching at one constant speed.
Reduce stride length before entering the opponent’s space.
Keep the eyes on the football while using peripheral vision to locate the opponent.
Arrive with the hips underneath the body.
Avoid jumping from too far away.
Approach beside the opponent rather than through their back.
Preserve the ability to jump, spoil or recover at ground level.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the defender reads the football early.
Whether acceleration occurs immediately.
Whether the defender decelerates before contact range.
Whether the final steps are balanced and adjustable.
Whether the defender approaches through the opponent’s back.
Whether the defender reaches spoiling distance without over-running the contest.

commonErrors.error: Defender approaches at full speed until contact.
commonErrors.correction: Shorten the final three steps and lower the centre of gravity.

commonErrors.error: Defender slows too early and cannot reach the contest.
commonErrors.correction: Accelerate through the first half of the approach.

commonErrors.error: Defender watches only the opponent.
commonErrors.correction: Pick up the football’s flight immediately and use peripheral vision.

commonErrors.error: Defender runs directly through the attacker’s back.
commonErrors.correction: Adjust the line to arrive beside the opponent.

commonErrors.error: Defender over-runs the drop zone.
commonErrors.correction: Reduce stride length as the football descends.

commonErrors.error: Defender jumps before establishing balance.
commonErrors.correction: Arrive on controlled feet before initiating the jump.

progressions: Permit the attacker to move within the contest zone.
Allow the defender to perform a controlled spoil.
Vary kick height and direction.
Begin the defender further away.
Add a second attacker to create traffic and decision pressure.
regressions: Use hand-thrown footballs with a predictable flight.
Rehearse the approach without a football.
successIndicators: Shorten the final steps before entering contact range.
Arrive balanced and beside the opponent.
Preserve the capacity to jump and recover.
matchApplication: Defenders regularly approach contests from several metres away after an opponent has created separation. Closing fast but arriving under control allows the defender to spoil legally, avoid giving away a free kick and remain involved if the football reaches ground level.
relatedDrills: SP-001 – Balanced Aerial Defence Starting Position

title: Spoil Timing Window
primarySkill: Timing the jump and spoiling action against the football’s flight.
objective: Teach defenders to delay their jump until they can make clean contact with the football at its highest reachable point.
groundSize: One 8 x 8-metre contest area per group.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations or several behaviours
setup:
Place an attacker and defender side by side inside the contest area.
The defender begins half a step behind and goal side.
A feeder stands 8–10 metres away.
The feeder delivers controlled high kicks or throws.
The attacker reaches for the football but does not initially jump at maximum intensity.
The defender performs a one-handed touch rather than a full-power spoil during introductory repetitions.
howTheDrillWorks:
The feeder delivers a high football towards the attacker.
The defender tracks the flight and moves into a balanced contesting position.
The attacker presents both hands as though attempting an overhead mark.
The defender waits until the football enters reachable range.
The defender jumps vertically or slightly forward and touches the football immediately before it reaches the attacker’s hands.
The defender lands on two balanced feet and turns towards the drop zone.
A successful repetition requires contact with the football without contacting the attacker’s head, arms or back.
Players rotate after five repetitions.
coachingPoints: Track the football from the feeder’s disposal.
Do not jump simply because the attacker begins to rise.
Time the action to the football rather than the opponent’s movement alone.
Reach towards the highest safe contact point.
Keep the spoiling arm strong but not locked.
Use the non-spoiling arm for balance without holding the opponent.
Jump from a stable base.
Land balanced and prepare for the next contest.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the defender jumps too early.
Whether the defender makes contact before the football reaches the attacker’s hands.
Whether the defender focuses on the football.
Whether contact is made with the opponent instead of the football.
Whether the defender lands safely.
Whether the defender immediately locates the drop zone.

commonErrors.error: Defender jumps before the football is reachable.
commonErrors.correction: Delay the jump and respond to the ball’s descent.

commonErrors.error: Defender swings down onto the attacker’s arms.
commonErrors.correction: Reach through the football at its highest safe point.

commonErrors.error: Defender contacts the opponent’s head or back.
commonErrors.correction: Adjust the starting line and attack the football from beside the opponent.

commonErrors.error: Defender jumps from an unstable base.
commonErrors.correction: Shorten the final steps and plant before jumping.

commonErrors.error: Defender closes the eyes at contact.
commonErrors.correction: Keep vision on the football until the hand makes contact.

commonErrors.error: Defender lands and stops.
commonErrors.correction: Turn immediately towards the football’s new location.

progressions: Allow the attacker to jump at full intensity.
Vary the height and speed of the delivery.
Require the defender to direct the spoil towards a nominated side.
Add a ground-level player who contests the resulting loose football.
Begin the defender from a moving approach.
regressions: Allow the defender to begin beside the attacker.
Keep both players grounded and practise the hand contact only.
Use a stationary ball held above shoulder height.
Reduce the attacker’s reach and movement.
successIndicators: Delay the jump until the football is reachable.
Contact the football before it reaches the attacker’s hands.
Reorient immediately towards the next phase.
matchApplication: Correct timing allows a defender to overcome a positional or height disadvantage without conceding a free kick. The defender must act late enough to reach the football but early enough to prevent the attacker from completing the mark.

title: Closed-Fist Spoiling Technique
primarySkill: Executing a safe and effective closed-fist spoil.
objective: Develop a strong closed-fist spoiling action that contacts the football cleanly without striking the opponent.
groundSize: 8 x 6-metre stations.
equipment: Optional suspended football or ball bag
coachingDifficulty: 2 – Basic coaching knowledge with one main teaching point
setup:
Players work in pairs with one football.
One player holds the football above head height with two hands.
The defender stands beside the holder at arm’s length.
The held football must remain clear of the holder’s head.
Additional stations may use a football suspended from a safe support.
The drill begins without jumping.
howTheDrillWorks:
The holder presents the football above and slightly in front of the defender.
The defender forms a firm fist with the thumb positioned outside the fingers.
The defender drives the fist through the centre or lower half of the football.
The shoulder and elbow extend in one direct action.
The defender finishes with the hand moving towards the intended spoil direction.
The holder resets the football after each repetition.
Complete five repetitions with each arm.
Players then change roles.
Once technique is stable, the holder gently tosses the football above the defender for a moving spoil.
coachingPoints: Close the fingers firmly with the thumb outside the fist.
Keep the wrist straight at contact.
Strike through the football rather than flicking at it.
Use a direct line from shoulder to ball.
Contact the football with the broad front surface of the fist.
Keep the eyes on the contact point.
Practise with both arms.
Direct the follow-through towards the safest available area.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the fist is formed safely.
Whether the wrist remains aligned.
Whether contact occurs through the centre of the football.
Whether the player swings across the body.
Whether both arms can perform the skill.
Whether the follow-through matches the intended spoil direction.

commonErrors.error: Thumb is trapped inside the fingers.
commonErrors.correction: Place the thumb securely across the outside of the fist.

commonErrors.error: Wrist bends at contact.
commonErrors.correction: Align the knuckles, wrist and forearm.

commonErrors.error: Player slaps at the football.
commonErrors.correction: Form a closed fist and drive directly through the ball.

commonErrors.error: Contact is made with the fingertips.
commonErrors.correction: Use the broad front surface of the fist.

commonErrors.error: Arm swings across the opponent’s space.
commonErrors.correction: Use a straight path towards the football.

commonErrors.error: Player can only spoil with the preferred arm.
commonErrors.correction: Alternate arms every repetition.

progressions: Add a small jump.
Have the feeder toss the football from different angles.
Require the player to direct the spoil left or right.
Add a passive marking opponent.
Perform the spoil after a short approach.
regressions: Hold the football at shoulder height.
Allow the defender to rehearse the fist and wrist position without contact.
Reduce the speed of the toss.
Practise only the preferred arm before alternating.
successIndicators: Drive through rather than slap at the football.
Use either arm according to the football’s position.
matchApplication: A clean closed-fist spoil creates stronger and more reliable contact than an uncontrolled slap. It allows the defender to reach through the football, reduce the likelihood of an opponent completing a mark and direct the football towards a safer location.

title: Full-Reach Contact Point
primarySkill: Reaching the highest safe point of the football during a spoil.
objective: Develop the defender’s ability to maximise reach and select the correct spoiling arm according to the football’s position.
groundSize: 10 x 8-metre stations.
equipment: Optional soft landing mats for introductory indoor work
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations or several behaviours
setup:
A feeder stands 6–8 metres from the defender.
Place two coloured markers to the defender’s left and right.
The feeder delivers a high throw or short kick towards either side of the defender.
The defender begins in a balanced stance.
A retriever stands behind the contest area.
No attacker is used during the first phase.
howTheDrillWorks:
The feeder delivers the football above either the defender’s left or right shoulder.
The defender tracks the football and takes one or two adjustment steps.
The defender selects the arm closest to the football.
The defender jumps and extends through the shoulder, elbow and wrist.
The fist contacts the football at the highest safe reachable point.
The spoil is directed towards the matching coloured marker.
The defender lands, regains balance and follows the football.
Players rotate through feeder, defender and retriever roles after six repetitions.
coachingPoints: Select the arm that provides the clearest and longest path to the football.
Avoid reaching across the body when the near-side arm is available.
Extend through the shoulder rather than relying only on the elbow.
Keep the head stable and eyes fixed on the football.
Jump from a balanced final step.
Reach upwards and through the football.
Use the non-spoiling arm for balance.
Land with knees flexed and feet prepared to move.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the defender selects the correct arm.
Whether the player reaches across the body unnecessarily.
Whether full shoulder and elbow extension is achieved.
Whether contact occurs near the highest reachable point.
Whether the player remains balanced in the air.
Whether the landing allows an immediate recovery effort.

commonErrors.error: Defender always uses the preferred arm.
commonErrors.correction: Match the arm to the side of the football.

commonErrors.error: Defender reaches across the body.
commonErrors.correction: Use the near-side arm and keep the chest underneath the contact point.

commonErrors.error: Jump begins before the feet are set.
commonErrors.correction: Take a controlled final step before leaving the ground.

commonErrors.error: Elbow remains bent at contact.
commonErrors.correction: Extend fully through shoulder and elbow.

commonErrors.error: Defender arches excessively in the air.
commonErrors.correction: Keep the ribs controlled and jump from underneath the football.

commonErrors.error: Landing is stiff or unstable.
commonErrors.correction: Land with soft knees and a balanced base.

progressions: Add a passive marking opponent.
Increase the delivery distance.
Vary the football’s height and lateral movement.
Require a second effort after landing.
Begin with a moving approach.
regressions: Permit the defender to nominate the arm before each feed.
Use a stationary football held at different positions.
successIndicators: Select the arm nearest the football.
Contact the football at the highest reachable point.
matchApplication: A defender is often required to spoil from a disadvantaged position and may have only one hand available. Maximising reach with the correct arm can be the difference between conceding a mark and forcing the football to ground.

title: Legal Bodywork Before the Ball Arrives
primarySkill: Using legal body positioning to protect the approach to an aerial contest.
objective: Teach defenders to use their hips, shoulders and ground position legally without holding, blocking or pushing the opponent.
groundSize: 10 x 8-metre contest areas.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations or several behaviours
setup:
Place an attacker and defender side by side approximately 5 metres from a marked drop zone.
A feeder stands 10 metres away.
The defender begins goal side and slightly behind.
The feeder initially holds the football while the pair practise movement into the drop zone.
Contact is limited to controlled hip and shoulder positioning.
Holding, pushing in the back, arm bars and front-on contact are prohibited.
howTheDrillWorks:
On the feeder’s call, the attacker and defender move towards the drop zone.
The defender attempts to establish a strong position beside the attacker.
The defender uses the hips and shoulder line to occupy space without extending the arms into the opponent.
The feeder calls “freeze” as the players enter the contest area.
The coach checks balance, goal-side position and legality.
Once the body position is consistently legal, the feeder delivers a controlled high football.
The defender maintains position and performs a controlled spoil.
The repetition ends when the football is spoiled or marked.
Players rotate after four contests.
coachingPoints: Win space with the feet before using the body.
Keep the arms free and avoid wrapping or holding.
Maintain a stable base through the hips and legs.
Apply contact from beside the opponent rather than through the back.
Keep the eyes connected to the football.
Do not initiate contact before reaching a legitimate contesting position.
Match force to the opponent’s movement.
Release body pressure when the football changes direction.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the defender moves the feet before initiating contact.
Whether contact is made with the hip or shoulder rather than the hands.
Whether the defender pushes in the back.
Whether the defender holds an arm or jumper.
Whether vision remains on the football.
Whether both players remain balanced and safe.

commonErrors.error: Defender reaches and holds the opponent.
commonErrors.correction: Remove the hands and regain position with the feet.

commonErrors.error: Defender pushes from behind.
commonErrors.correction: Move beside the opponent before applying body pressure.

commonErrors.error: Defender braces with extended forearms.
commonErrors.correction: Keep the elbows close and use the shoulder and hip line.

commonErrors.error: Defender watches only the opponent.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain vision of the football while feeling the opponent’s position.

commonErrors.error: Defender initiates heavy contact too early.
commonErrors.correction: Delay body pressure until both players are approaching the contest.

commonErrors.error: Defender becomes upright and loses balance.
commonErrors.correction: Lower the hips and widen the base slightly.

progressions: Allow the attacker to change the approach line.
Increase the delivery distance.
Permit realistic marking and spoiling efforts.
Add a second defender who provides cover.
Begin from a moving one-on-one lead.
regressions: Use freeze points before any football is delivered.
Remove the jump and complete the contest at ground level.
Reduce contact for younger or returning players.
successIndicators: Use legal hip and shoulder contact.
Avoid holding, blocking and pushing in the back.
Remain balanced while tracking the football.
Progress from body position into a legitimate aerial contest.
matchApplication: Legal bodywork allows a defender to influence an opponent’s run and protect access to the drop zone without conceding a free kick. It is essential when defending one-on-one contests inside defensive 50, along the boundary and during long kicks to a contest.

title: Directional Spoil to Safety
primarySkill: Directing a spoil towards a tactically safe area.
objective: Develop the defender’s ability to direct the football away from dangerous central space and towards a boundary, teammate or low-risk area.
groundSize: 15 x 12-metre contest areas with three marked exit zones.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations or several behaviours
setup:
Mark a central danger zone behind the contest.
Mark two safer spoil zones to the left and right.
Position an attacker and defender in the central contest area.
A feeder stands 12–15 metres away.
A supporting defender stands outside one safe zone.
The coach nominates the boundary side or safe exit before early repetitions.
howTheDrillWorks:
The feeder delivers a high football towards the attacker.
The defender approaches and establishes a legal contesting position.
Before jumping, the defender scans or listens for the supporting defender’s call.
The defender selects the appropriate spoiling arm.
The defender contacts the football and directs it towards a safe zone.
A spoil into a safe zone scores two points.
A spoil that drops directly in front of goal or into the central danger zone scores no points.
The supporting defender collects any football entering their zone.
Players reset and rotate after four contests.
coachingPoints: Identify the dangerous and safe sides before the football arrives.
Use the hand and contact angle that support the intended direction.
Avoid spoiling directly back into the corridor.
When uncertain, create distance and width.
Use the boundary as a defensive advantage where appropriate.
Listen for communication from supporting defenders.
Do not sacrifice clean contact by attempting an unrealistic direction.
Recover immediately if the football does not reach the intended zone.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the defender identifies the safe area before jumping.
Whether the correct arm is selected.
Whether the follow-through directs the football.
Whether the defender prioritises clean contact.
Whether supporting players communicate.
Whether the defender recovers when the spoil falls short.

commonErrors.error: Spoil is directed back towards goal.
commonErrors.correction: Angle the contact and follow-through towards the boundary side.

commonErrors.error: Defender attempts excessive direction and misses the football.
commonErrors.correction: Prioritise contact first, then add direction.

commonErrors.error: Defender uses the wrong arm.
commonErrors.correction: Select the arm nearest the safe side of the football.

commonErrors.error: Defender does not scan the field.
commonErrors.correction: Identify the danger and safe zones before the kick arrives.

commonErrors.error: Supporting defender remains silent.
commonErrors.correction: Call the preferred spoil side early and repeatedly.

commonErrors.error: Defender admires the spoil.
commonErrors.correction: Land and move immediately towards the next contest.

progressions: Remove the coach’s nominated safe side.
Add an attacking ground-level player in the danger zone.
Award bonus points when a teammate gathers the directed spoil.
Vary the field position and boundary orientation.
Allow the attacker to lead across the contest area.
regressions: Nominate the spoil direction before each repetition.
Increase the size of the safe zones.
successIndicators: Make clean contact with the football.
Direct the spoil away from central danger.
Connect the aerial action with supporting defenders.
matchApplication: A spoil that merely prevents a mark may still create a scoring opportunity for the opposition. Directing the football towards the boundary, a teammate or a less dangerous area improves the likelihood that the defensive team will win the next possession or force a stoppage.
relatedDrills: SP-007 – Legal Bodywork Before the Ball Arrives

title: Spoil and Ground-Level Recovery
primarySkill: Recovering immediately after an aerial spoil.
objective: Develop the habit of landing, locating the football and contributing to the next contest immediately after spoiling.
groundSize: 15 x 12-metre contest areas.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations or several behaviours
setup:
Position one attacker and one defender in an aerial contest area.
Place one ground-level support player from each team 3–5 metres outside the contest.
A feeder stands 12–15 metres away.
Mark two defensive exit gates on the boundary side.
The defender’s team attacks the exit gates after winning the loose football.
Contact is controlled and all tackling must follow previously established safety standards.
howTheDrillWorks:
The feeder delivers a high football to the aerial contest.
The defender attempts to spoil the football away from the attacker.
Both aerial players must land safely before joining the ground-level contest.
The two support players react to the football’s direction.
The defender’s team attempts to gather and move the football through either exit gate.
The attacking team attempts to regain possession and handball to the feeder.
The phase continues for a maximum of eight seconds.
Two points are awarded for a successful spoil followed by a defensive exit.
One point is awarded for a spoil that forces a stoppage or boundary result.
Players rotate through aerial, support and feeder roles.
coachingPoints: Land with the feet underneath the body.
Find the football immediately rather than watching the opponent.
Take the shortest effective line to the loose football.
Communicate who will gather and who will protect.
Stay involved even if the spoil travels away from the original contest.
Avoid diving recklessly into the legs of another player.
Use a clean first disposal when the football is won.
Reapply pressure immediately if the opposition gathers.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the defender lands safely.
How quickly the defender locates the football.
Whether the defender joins the next contest.
Whether teammates communicate gathering and protection roles.
Whether the defensive team exits towards safety.
Whether players maintain legal and controlled ground-level contact.

commonErrors.error: Defender watches the result of the spoil.
commonErrors.correction: Locate the football before completing the landing.

commonErrors.error: Defender remains out of the ground contest.
commonErrors.correction: Take an immediate second-effort line towards the football or opponent.

commonErrors.error: Two defenders attack the football and leave no protection.
commonErrors.correction: Call one player to gather and one to protect.

commonErrors.error: Exit disposal returns to central danger.
commonErrors.correction: Use the boundary-side gate or safest visible option.

commonErrors.error: Player dives head-first into congestion.
commonErrors.correction: Stay on the feet where possible and approach with control.

commonErrors.error: Defender gives up after the attacker gathers.
commonErrors.correction: Reapply pressure and attempt to force a turnover or stoppage.

progressions: Remove the eight-second phase limit.
Add another support player to each team.
Permit the feeder to join the attacking phase.
Begin from a moving lead.
Add a second disposal requirement before the defensive exit scores.
regressions: Stop the drill immediately after the defender gathers.
Direct the initial spoil towards a nominated area.
Reduce the size and speed of the aerial contest.
successIndicators: Convert the spoil into possession, territory or a stoppage.
matchApplication: Aerial defence does not finish when the football is punched away. Inside defensive 50, the next ground-level possession often determines whether the opposition scores. Defenders must recover quickly, support teammates and move the football towards a safe exit.
relatedDrills: TK-120 – Tackling and Pressure Chapter Final Assessment

title: Aerial Defence Fundamentals Circuit
primarySkill: Integrating fundamental aerial-defence techniques across multiple stations.
objective: Assess and reinforce the defender’s ability to combine the fundamental skills required to prepare for, execute and recover from an aerial spoil.
groundSize: Four stations positioned across approximately one-third of the ground.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Create four stations with equal player groups.
Station 1 tests starting position and goal-side movement.
Station 2 tests controlled approach and spoil timing.
Station 3 tests closed-fist contact, arm selection and spoil direction.
Station 4 tests legal bodywork, aerial spoil and ground-level recovery.
Assign one coach or experienced leader to each station where possible.
Players complete each station for four to five minutes before rotating.
Use controlled deliveries suitable for the age and ability of the group.
howTheDrillWorks:
At Station 1, the defender establishes a balanced position and responds to an attacker’s lead while remaining goal side.
At Station 2, the defender approaches a stationary or lightly moving attacker and times a controlled spoil.
At Station 3, the feeder varies the football’s position and the defender selects the correct arm to direct the spoil towards a safe zone.
At Station 4, the defender uses legal body positioning, spoils and then joins a short ground-level contest.
Each defender receives up to five points at each station.
Coaches score starting position, approach, legality, football contact and recovery behaviour.
Players receive one immediate coaching correction before repeating the task.
Groups rotate clockwise when the coach signals.
The circuit concludes with a short review of the most consistent strengths and common errors.
coachingPoints: Establish position before reacting to the football.
Protect goal side and dangerous space.
Close quickly but arrive balanced.
Time the jump to the football.
Use a strong closed fist and the correct arm.
Make the football the primary target.
Direct the spoil towards a safer area.
Land, recover and contribute to the next contest.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the player applies the same starting-position habits across stations.
Whether approach speed is controlled.
Whether the spoil is timed and technically sound.
Whether contact with the opponent remains legal.
Whether the player can use either arm.
Whether the football is directed intelligently.
Whether the player completes a second effort.
Whether technique deteriorates as fatigue increases.

commonErrors.error: Player treats each station as an unrelated activity.
commonErrors.correction: Reinforce the sequence: position, approach, spoil, recover.

commonErrors.error: Defender prioritises contact with the opponent.
commonErrors.correction: Re-centre attention on the football and legal contesting position.

commonErrors.error: Spoil technique breaks down under movement.
commonErrors.correction: Reduce approach speed and rebuild the final steps.

commonErrors.error: Defender always spoils in the same direction.
commonErrors.correction: Scan the field and use the appropriate arm and follow-through.

commonErrors.error: Defender stops after the aerial contest.
commonErrors.correction: Require an immediate recovery action before awarding the score.

commonErrors.error: Fatigue creates unsafe bodywork.
commonErrors.correction: Reduce repetitions, extend recovery and restore technical control.

progressions: Convert the stations into continuous competitive games.
Add live leading patterns at each station.
Introduce a second defender and require communication.
Use field-position-specific safe and dangerous zones.
Finish with a conditioned small-sided game in which defenders score for effective spoils and exits.
regressions: Score only one technical priority at each station.
Pair developing players with experienced leaders.
successIndicators: Establish an effective defensive starting position.
Time and execute a legal spoil.
Recover immediately and contribute to the next phase.
matchApplication: The circuit connects the full sequence required in match play. Defenders must begin in the correct position, read the kick, close space, contest legally, direct the football away from danger and remain involved when the football reaches ground level. The drill provides an introductory assessment before the chapter progresses into more complex movement, pressure and tactical aerial-defence situations.
relatedDrills: SP-001 – Balanced Aerial Defence Starting Position

title: Rear-Position Reach Spoil
primarySkill: Spoiling effectively from behind an opponent without infringing.
objective: Develop the defender’s ability to remain composed when positioned behind an opponent and reach cleanly over or beside the contest to contact the football without pushing in the back or striking the opponent’s arms.
groundSize: One 10 x 8-metre contest area per group.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations or several behaviours
setup:
Place an attacker 8–10 metres from a feeder.
Position the defender approximately half a metre behind the attacker.
Mark a 3-metre contest zone around the expected drop point.
The feeder delivers controlled, high footballs towards the attacker.
The attacker attempts an overhead mark but must maintain a straight approach line during introductory repetitions.
The defender may contact the football only and must not use two hands to push or hold the opponent.
howTheDrillWorks:
The feeder delivers a high football towards the attacker.
The attacker moves into the drop zone and prepares to mark.
The defender closes the final distance while maintaining balance.
The defender identifies whether the football can be reached over the attacker’s shoulder or from the side.
The defender jumps late and extends one arm towards the football.
The defender contacts the football before it reaches the attacker’s hands.
The defender lands, locates the football and moves towards the next contest.
The repetition ends after the defender completes a second effort or the attacker secures the mark.
Players rotate after four to six contests.
coachingPoints: Avoid panic when starting behind the opponent.
Close enough to influence the contest without running through the opponent’s back.
Keep the chest upright rather than leaning heavily onto the attacker.
Reach beside or over the opponent’s shoulder according to the football’s position.
Time the jump to the football rather than copying the attacker’s jump.
Keep the non-spoiling arm free and away from the opponent’s body.
Contact the football with a strong closed fist.
Land and recover immediately.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the defender closes the space before the jump.
Whether the defender leans or pushes into the opponent’s back.
Whether the correct arm is selected.
Whether the defender contacts the football rather than the opponent’s forearms.
Whether the defender jumps too early.
Whether the defender remains involved after landing.

commonErrors.error: Defender pushes the opponent in the back.
commonErrors.correction: Keep the torso upright and reach to the football without extending through the opponent.

commonErrors.error: Defender swings down onto the opponent’s arms.
commonErrors.correction: Reach above the hands and contact the football at its highest reachable point.

commonErrors.error: Defender jumps too early.
commonErrors.correction: Wait until the football is entering the contesting window.

commonErrors.error: Defender remains too far behind to reach.
commonErrors.correction: Close the final metre before beginning the jump.

commonErrors.error: Defender uses the far arm and reaches across the opponent.
commonErrors.correction: Select the arm nearest the football’s path.

commonErrors.error: Defender stops after the spoil.
commonErrors.correction: Land, locate the football and complete a second effort.

progressions: Allow the attacker to use a curved or angled lead.
Vary the football’s height and lateral movement.
Add a ground-level player from each team.
Require the defender to direct the spoil towards a nominated safe zone.
Begin the defender two metres behind and require a controlled closing approach.
regressions: Begin the defender beside the attacker.
Allow the defender to touch rather than punch the football.
successIndicators: Avoid pushing or holding the opponent.
Contact the football before the mark is completed.
Land safely and continue into the next phase.
matchApplication: Defenders are frequently required to recover after an opponent gains separation on a lead. A controlled reach spoil from behind can prevent a mark without conceding a free kick and allows the defender to remain involved when the football reaches ground level.
relatedDrills: SP-007 – Legal Bodywork Before the Ball Arrives

title: Front-Position Aerial Protection
primarySkill: Defending an aerial ball while positioned in front of an opponent.
objective: Teach defenders to protect front position, judge the football over their shoulder and prevent the opponent from gaining uncontested access to the drop zone.
groundSize: 12 x 10-metre channels.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations or several behaviours
setup:
Position the defender one metre in front of the attacker.
Place a feeder 12–15 metres away facing the pair.
Mark a 4-metre drop zone behind the defender.
The defender begins with the body half-open so the feeder and attacker can both be monitored.
The feeder delivers footballs over or slightly to either side of the defender.
Contact is controlled and neither player may hold or block with extended arms.
howTheDrillWorks:
The feeder prepares to deliver a high football towards the marked drop zone.
The defender checks the attacker’s location and opens the body towards the flight.
As the football is delivered, the defender uses drop steps to move backwards without turning completely away from the ball.
The attacker attempts to move into the marking line.
The defender protects the direct route to the drop zone using legal body position.
The defender judges whether to mark, spoil backwards or spoil laterally.
The contest ends when the football is marked, spoiled or reaches ground level.
Both players complete a recovery effort towards the loose football.
Roles rotate after five contests.
coachingPoints: Maintain front position without becoming stationary.
Use a half-open stance to see the football and feel the opponent’s movement.
Move with drop steps rather than running backwards upright.
Protect the direct line to the football.
Avoid backing underneath the flight and losing balance.
Do not extend the arms to hold the opponent out.
Judge whether the ball can be marked or must be spoiled.
Keep the spoil away from central danger.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the defender can maintain vision of the football.
Whether backward movement is balanced.
Whether the defender protects the direct path to the drop zone.
Whether the defender blocks illegally with extended arms.
Whether the defender judges the flight accurately.
Whether the correct mark-or-spoil decision is made.

commonErrors.error: Defender backpedals upright and loses balance.
commonErrors.correction: Turn the hips and use controlled drop steps.

commonErrors.error: Defender turns completely towards the opponent.
commonErrors.correction: Keep the chest half-open to the feeder and track the flight.

commonErrors.error: Defender allows the attacker to run directly through the drop zone.
commonErrors.correction: Protect the straight line with the feet and body position.

commonErrors.error: Defender holds the opponent out with both arms.
commonErrors.correction: Keep the arms free and occupy space legally with the body.

commonErrors.error: Defender moves too far under the football.
commonErrors.correction: Stay slightly in front of the drop point and judge the descent.

commonErrors.error: Defender spoils when an uncontested mark is available.
commonErrors.correction: Assess the opponent’s pressure before deciding to punch.

progressions: Allow the attacker to change direction before entering the drop zone.
Add a supporting defender who communicates the opponent’s movement.
Vary the kick between shallow and deep trajectories.
Add a scoring consequence for a spoil into central danger.
Continue into a live ground-level contest.
regressions: Keep the attacker at walking pace.
Mark the defender’s backward movement path with cones.
Allow the defender to call the expected drop point before the contest.
successIndicators: Track the football while monitoring the opponent.
Protect the direct route to the drop zone.
matchApplication: Front-position aerial defence is essential when a defender has read the kick early or is protecting space behind the defensive line. The defender must remain balanced, deny the opponent a direct run and decide whether to intercept, mark or spoil.
relatedDrills: SP-001 – Balanced Aerial Defence Starting Position
SP-007 – Legal Bodywork Before the Ball Arrives

title: Side-On Shoulder Spoil
primarySkill: Spoiling from a side-on position while maintaining legal shoulder-to-shoulder alignment.
objective: Develop the defender’s ability to contest from beside an opponent and use the near-side arm to spoil cleanly without crossing through the opponent’s body.
groundSize: 10 x 10-metre contest areas.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations or several behaviours
setup:
Place an attacker and defender shoulder to shoulder in the centre of the contest area.
The defender begins on either the attacker’s left or right side.
A feeder stands 8–12 metres away.
The feeder delivers the football towards the attacker’s outside shoulder.
The defender must use the arm closest to the football.
Body contact is restricted to controlled shoulder and hip contact.
howTheDrillWorks:
The feeder nominates or visually indicates the delivery side.
The attacker and defender move towards the expected drop point.
The defender establishes shoulder-to-shoulder position.
The defender keeps the hips underneath the body and avoids leaning across the attacker.
As the football descends, the defender jumps and uses the near-side arm to spoil.
The defender directs the football away from the attacker’s preferred side.
Both players land and react to the football.
Players alternate starting sides after each repetition.
Roles rotate after six contests.
coachingPoints: Arrive beside the opponent rather than behind or across them.
Maintain a strong shoulder-to-shoulder line.
Use the arm nearest the football.
Keep the non-spoiling arm free and legal.
Avoid reaching across the opponent’s head or chest.
Jump vertically from a balanced base.
Direct the football away from the attacker’s front.
Recover immediately after landing.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the defender establishes legal side-on position.
Whether the correct arm is selected.
Whether the defender leans across the opponent.
Whether the defender remains balanced during contact.
Whether the spoil is directed safely.
Whether the defender follows the football after landing.

commonErrors.error: Defender reaches across the opponent with the far arm.
commonErrors.correction: Use the arm nearest the football.

commonErrors.error: Defender approaches from behind and contacts the back.
commonErrors.correction: Adjust the line to arrive shoulder to shoulder.

commonErrors.error: Defender leans heavily across the opponent.
commonErrors.correction: Keep the chest over the hips and jump vertically.

commonErrors.error: Defender uses the free arm to hold.
commonErrors.correction: Keep the non-spoiling hand open and away from the opponent.

commonErrors.error: Spoil drops directly in front of the attacker.
commonErrors.correction: Angle the fist and follow-through away from the opponent’s front.

commonErrors.error: Defender loses balance after contact.
commonErrors.correction: Shorten the final steps and stabilise before jumping.

progressions: Allow the attacker to change sides during the approach.
Vary the delivery to either shoulder without warning.
Add ground-level support players.
Require the defender to spoil towards a nominated teammate.
Increase the run-up distance.
regressions: Nominate the spoiling arm before the delivery.
successIndicators: Direct the spoil away from the attacker’s advantage.
matchApplication: Many aerial contests occur with players arriving side by side. A defender who wins shoulder position and uses the correct arm can spoil effectively while reducing the risk of high contact, holding or pushing in the back.
relatedDrills: SP-007 – Legal Bodywork Before the Ball Arrives

title: Emergency Double-Fist Spoil
primarySkill: Executing a controlled two-fist spoil when maximum distance is required.
objective: Teach defenders to use a safe and powerful two-fist spoil when the tactical priority is to create maximum distance from a dangerous aerial contest.
groundSize: 12 x 10-metre stations.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations or several behaviours
setup:
Mark distance zones at 5, 10 and 15 metres from the contest point.
Position a defender beneath or approaching the contest point.
A feeder stands 10–15 metres away.
A passive attacker provides a marking target during later repetitions.
The defender practises joining both fists safely before full-speed execution.
The football is delivered high enough to permit a balanced jump.
howTheDrillWorks:
The feeder delivers a high football towards the contest point.
The defender moves underneath the football and establishes balance.
The defender forms two closed fists with the thumbs positioned safely.
The fists are brought together to create a broad contact surface.
The defender jumps and drives both fists through the lower half of the football.
The football is directed away from the scoring area and towards the distance zones.
The defender lands with both feet balanced and follows the football.
One point is awarded for 5 metres of clearance, two points for 10 metres and three points for 15 metres or more.
Players rotate after five repetitions.
coachingPoints: Use two fists only when maximum distance is tactically required.
Join the fists securely without interlocking the fingers.
Keep both wrists straight.
Contact the lower half of the football to produce distance.
Extend through both shoulders and elbows.
Avoid swinging down towards an opponent’s head or arms.
Jump from directly underneath or slightly behind the ball.
Land with the feet underneath the body.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether both fists are formed safely.
Whether the fists remain connected at contact.
Whether the defender contacts the football cleanly.
Whether the spoil creates useful distance.
Whether the defender over-swings downwards.
Whether the landing remains controlled.

commonErrors.error: Fingers are interlocked.
commonErrors.correction: Form two separate fists and press them together.

commonErrors.error: Wrists collapse at contact.
commonErrors.correction: Align both wrists with the forearms.

commonErrors.error: Defender contacts the top of the football.
commonErrors.correction: Strike through the lower half to create distance.

commonErrors.error: Arms swing down towards the opponent.
commonErrors.correction: Drive upwards and through the football.

commonErrors.error: Defender uses two fists when one hand would provide better direction.
commonErrors.correction: Reserve the technique for emergency clearance situations.

commonErrors.error: Defender lands heavily and cannot recover.
commonErrors.correction: Jump from balance and land with soft knees.

progressions: Add an active marking opponent.
Deliver footballs from different angles.
Require the clearance to avoid a central danger zone.
Add attacking ground-level players to punish short spoils.
Begin the defender from a moving approach.
regressions: Score only clean contact rather than distance.
successIndicators: Form a safe two-fist contact surface.
Direct the football away from the most dangerous area.
matchApplication: A two-fist spoil is appropriate when the football must be cleared from the goal square, the top of the goal square or another high-risk area. It should be used selectively because it creates distance but offers less directional precision than a one-handed spoil.

title: Boundary-Side Aerial Defence
primarySkill: Using the boundary as a defensive advantage in an aerial contest.
objective: Develop the defender’s ability to position the opponent towards the boundary and direct the aerial contest away from the corridor and central scoring space.
groundSize: 20 x 12-metre channel positioned along a boundary line.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Mark a boundary line along one side of the channel.
Mark a central danger zone on the opposite side.
Position an attacker and defender 12–15 metres from a feeder.
The defender begins goal side and slightly corridor side of the attacker.
A supporting defender starts 5 metres inside the field.
The feeder delivers high footballs towards the boundary-side contest.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacker attempts to lead towards either the boundary or the central side of the channel.
The defender uses starting position and footwork to discourage the central lead.
The feeder delivers the football once the lead begins.
The defender closes to the contest while maintaining corridor-side position.
The defender attempts to spoil towards the boundary or supporting defender.
A spoil across the boundary or into the boundary safety zone scores two points.
A spoil to the supporting defender scores three points.
A spoil into the central danger zone awards one point to the attacking team.
The phase continues at ground level for five seconds.
Players rotate after four contests.
coachingPoints: Position on the opponent’s corridor side.
Encourage the lead towards the boundary.
Do not allow the opponent to turn back into central space uncontested.
Use the nearest arm to direct the spoil.
Prioritise a boundary result when clean possession is unlikely.
Communicate with the supporting defender.
Avoid spoiling back over the corridor-side shoulder.
Recover inside the opponent after the contest.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the defender begins on the correct side.
Whether the attacker is influenced towards the boundary.
Whether the defender’s approach protects central space.
Whether the spoil is directed safely.
Whether supporting defenders communicate.
Whether the defender recovers goal side after the contest.

commonErrors.error: Defender starts boundary side and concedes the corridor.
commonErrors.correction: Move to the opponent’s corridor-side shoulder.

commonErrors.error: Defender follows the attacker outside but spoils back inside.
commonErrors.correction: Angle the fist and follow-through towards the boundary.

commonErrors.error: Defender attacks the football from directly behind.
commonErrors.correction: Close beside the attacker on the central side.

commonErrors.error: Supporting defender remains passive.
commonErrors.correction: Communicate early and position for the inside ground ball.

commonErrors.error: Defender attempts to mark in a heavily disadvantaged contest.
commonErrors.correction: Prioritise a safe spoil or boundary result.

commonErrors.error: Defender recovers outside the opponent.
commonErrors.correction: Land and move immediately to the goal-side or corridor-side position.

progressions: Allow the attacker to use double leads.
Add a second attacker in the central danger zone.
Remove the predetermined feeder and use live ball movement.
Require the defensive team to exit through a boundary-side gate.
Begin from a turnover in the corridor.
regressions: Restrict the attacker to a boundary lead.
successIndicators: Influence the opponent towards the boundary.
Arrive in a legal contesting position.
Direct the football away from central danger.
Recover inside and goal side after the spoil.
matchApplication: Boundary-side aerial defence reduces the opponent’s attacking options and gives the defender a predictable safe side. It is especially valuable when defending wide forward entries, down-the-line kicks and exits from defensive 50.

title: Long-Kick Drop-Zone Defence
primarySkill: Reading and defending the drop zone of a long aerial kick.
objective: Develop the defender’s ability to identify the likely drop zone of a long kick, arrive early and establish the most effective position before the aerial contest forms.
groundSize: A 30 x 25-metre area.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Mark three possible drop zones across the width of the area.
Position two attackers and two defenders 20–25 metres from the kicker.
The kicker may deliver to any of the three zones.
Defenders begin in different positions so one may be closer to the expected drop point.
One coach or player stands behind the contest to observe positioning.
Contact remains controlled during early repetitions.
howTheDrillWorks:
The kicker scans the three target zones and selects one without announcing it.
All players track the football from the moment of disposal.
The defenders identify the likely drop zone and communicate who will contest.
The primary defender moves to establish front, side or rear position according to the flight.
The supporting defender positions to protect the dangerous ground-level space.
The attackers attempt to mark or bring the football to advantage.
The primary defender marks or spoils according to the contest.
Play continues for eight seconds after the football reaches ground level.
The defensive team scores for an intercept mark, safe spoil or controlled exit.
Roles rotate after five deliveries.
coachingPoints: Read the football’s trajectory immediately after the kick.
Move towards the drop zone rather than chasing the opponent.
Communicate early about who will contest.
The earliest defender should establish the strongest aerial position.
The supporting defender should protect the front and central ground ball.
Avoid two defenders flying for the same football without communication.
Judge whether the ball will fall short, carry over the back or hold in the air.
Complete the contest through the ground-level phase.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
How early defenders read the football’s flight.
Whether defenders run to the drop zone or follow opponents.
Whether communication identifies the primary aerial defender.
Whether supporting position is maintained.
Whether defenders make appropriate mark-or-spoil decisions.
Whether the defensive team controls the next possession.

commonErrors.error: Defender follows the opponent rather than reading the ball.
commonErrors.correction: Track the flight and move directly towards the drop zone.

commonErrors.error: Both defenders fly for the same football.
commonErrors.correction: Call the primary defender early and protect the ground with the second defender.

commonErrors.error: Defender arrives underneath the football.
commonErrors.correction: Adjust earlier and remain slightly goal side of the drop point.

commonErrors.error: Supporting defender stands directly behind the contest.
commonErrors.correction: Position in front or on the dangerous central side.

commonErrors.error: Defender guesses the drop zone before the kick.
commonErrors.correction: React to the football’s actual trajectory.

commonErrors.error: Players stop after the spoil.
commonErrors.correction: Continue until the football is secured, cleared or a stoppage is formed.

progressions: Increase the kicking distance.
Add a third attacker and defender.
Use live ball movement before the long kick.
Introduce wind or wet-weather decision rules where safe.
Add scoring zones that reflect defensive 50 exits.
regressions: Nominate the target zone before the kick.
Allow defenders to begin closer to the drop zone.
Stop play after the aerial contest.
successIndicators: Identify the likely drop zone early.
Establish effective position before the opponent.
Make a clean mark or effective spoil.
Complete the defensive phase after the ball reaches ground level.
matchApplication: Long kicks create aerial contests where early judgement is more important than raw speed. Defenders who identify the drop zone first can establish front position, coordinate support and reduce the opposition’s ability to mark or win the ground ball.

title: Aerial Defender Communication
primarySkill: Communicating roles between defenders before and during an aerial contest.
objective: Develop clear communication that identifies the aerial contestant, supporting defender and dangerous ground-level space before the football arrives.
groundSize: 25 x 20-metre area.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Create groups containing two defenders, two attackers and one feeder.
Mark a central aerial contest area and two ground-level danger zones.
Defenders begin 4–6 metres apart.
Attackers may lead into the same or different areas.
The feeder delivers a high football to either attacker.
Defenders must communicate before entering the contest.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attackers begin moving on the feeder’s signal.
The feeder selects one attacker and delivers a high football.
Defenders scan the football and opponents.
One defender calls “mine” or another agreed team call to claim the aerial contest.
The second defender acknowledges the call and moves to protect the front, central or goal-side ground space.
The primary defender attempts to mark or spoil.
The supporting defender reacts to the outcome and attempts to secure the loose football.
If neither defender communicates before the contest, the attacking team receives one point.
The defensive team receives points for clear communication followed by a successful defensive outcome.
Players rotate after four to six contests.
coachingPoints: Communicate early enough to change teammates’ movement.
Use one clear and consistent team call.
The player with the best line and view should claim the aerial contest.
The supporting defender must acknowledge the call.
Avoid vague calls such as “go” or “leave” without context.
Support in front and towards the most dangerous space.
Continue communication after the spoil.
Review responsibility immediately after each repetition.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether communication occurs before the jump.
Whether the correct defender claims the contest.
Whether the supporting defender responds to the call.
Whether two defenders fly unnecessarily.
Whether dangerous ground space is protected.
Whether communication continues after the football reaches ground level.

commonErrors.error: Call is made after both defenders have committed.
commonErrors.correction: Communicate as soon as the drop zone and best contestant are identified.

commonErrors.error: Both defenders call for the football.
commonErrors.correction: The player with the strongest line makes the first decisive call.

commonErrors.error: Supporting defender remains beside the aerial contest.
commonErrors.correction: Move to the front or dangerous ground-level space.

commonErrors.error: Defender uses unclear language.
commonErrors.correction: Use one agreed team call consistently.

commonErrors.error: Supporting defender does not acknowledge the call.
commonErrors.correction: Require a verbal response before the contest continues.

commonErrors.error: Players stop communicating after the spoil.
commonErrors.correction: Direct the next gather, pressure and exit action.

progressions: Add a third defender and attacker.
Begin from live ball movement.
Allow the feeder to kick short or long.
Add a goalkeeper who organises the defenders.
Continue until the defensive team exits the area.
regressions: Nominate the primary defender before the kick.
Pause play after the call to check positions.
successIndicators: Acknowledge and respond to the call.
Continue directing teammates after the spoil.
matchApplication: Defensive aerial contests are rarely isolated. Clear communication prevents teammates from colliding, ensures one player attacks the football and positions others to defend the likely ground ball or opposition crumber.

title: Two-Defender Aerial Coverage
primarySkill: Coordinating aerial and ground-level responsibilities between two defenders.
objective: Teach two defenders to work as a connected unit, with one attacking the aerial football and the other protecting dangerous space and supporting the next phase.
groundSize: 25 x 20-metre area.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Position two attackers and two defenders in the playing area.
Place a feeder 20 metres away.
Mark a central danger zone and two defensive exit gates.
One attacker presents aerially while the other positions for the ground ball.
Defenders begin side by side or in a shallow stagger.
The feeder may kick to either attacker.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attackers move as the feeder prepares to kick.
The defenders scan and communicate their responsibilities.
The defender with the best line attacks the aerial football.
The second defender moves to protect the front, goal side or likely spoil direction.
The aerial defender attempts to mark or spoil.
The supporting defender attempts to secure the loose football or pressure the attacking ground player.
If the defensive team wins possession, it exits through either gate.
If the attacking team wins possession, it attempts to handball to the feeder.
Play continues for a maximum of ten seconds.
Players rotate after four possessions.
coachingPoints: Identify aerial and support roles early.
Do not allow both defenders to be drawn underneath the same football.
The support player should position according to the likely spoil direction.
Protect the front and central side first.
Maintain goal-side balance across the pair.
Communicate changes if the flight moves away from the original contestant.
Use the first clean possession to exit danger.
Reapply pressure immediately after a lost contest.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the defenders establish separate roles.
Whether the correct defender contests aerially.
Whether the support defender protects dangerous space.
Whether the pair remain connected after the spoil.
Whether both defenders become attracted to the football.
Whether possession is converted into a safe exit.

commonErrors.error: Both defenders fly for the football.
commonErrors.correction: Nominate one contestant and keep the second defender grounded.

commonErrors.error: Supporting defender stands behind the contest.
commonErrors.correction: Move to the front or central side where the loose football is most dangerous.

commonErrors.error: Defenders fail to adjust when the kick changes direction.
commonErrors.correction: Continue communicating and transfer the aerial role if required.

commonErrors.error: Support defender watches rather than reacts.
commonErrors.correction: Move as the aerial player begins the spoil.

commonErrors.error: Defensive exit is rushed into pressure.
commonErrors.correction: Secure possession and use the safest available gate.

commonErrors.error: Defenders separate after the contest.
commonErrors.correction: Recover together and maintain mutual support.

progressions: Add a third attacker and defender.
Use live ball movement before the entry.
Allow the aerial attacker to bring the ball to ground deliberately.
Add a scoring target behind the defensive exit gates.
Increase contact to match-like levels for appropriate groups.
regressions: Nominate the aerial defender before each kick.
Direct the spoil towards the supporting defender.
successIndicators: Send one defender to the aerial contest.
Convert defensive possession into a controlled exit.
matchApplication: Two defenders must operate as a system rather than independently. One contests the football while the other protects the ground, supports the spoil and provides the first outlet from defensive congestion.

title: Mark-or-Spoil Decision
primarySkill: Deciding whether to mark or spoil an aerial football.
objective: Develop the defender’s ability to assess pressure, field position and football flight before choosing to mark, spoil or bring the football safely to ground.
groundSize: 20 x 15-metre area.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Position one defender and one attacker in the central contest area.
A feeder stands 12–18 metres away.
A supporting defender stands near an exit gate.
The attacker varies pressure from passive to full contest according to the coach’s signal.
The feeder varies the flight between uncontested, marginal and clearly disadvantaged situations.
The defender is not told in advance whether to mark or spoil.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach privately signals the attacker’s pressure level.
The feeder delivers a high football towards the contest area.
The defender reads the football’s flight and checks the attacker’s position.
If clearly in front and balanced, the defender attempts to mark.
If under significant pressure or out of position, the defender spoils towards safety.
If the football is unable to be marked cleanly, the defender brings it to ground away from central danger.
Play continues until the defensive team exits through a gate or the attacking team wins possession.
The defender receives two points for the correct decision and one additional point for successful execution.
The coach provides immediate feedback on decision quality rather than outcome alone.
Players rotate after five contests.
coachingPoints: Assess the opponent’s proximity before deciding.
Mark when the football can be secured cleanly.
Spoil when the risk of being outmarked is high.
Consider field position and the danger of a dropped mark.
Do not punch away uncontested intercept opportunities.
Do not attempt low-percentage marks from a disadvantaged position.
Direct the spoil towards support or the boundary.
Complete the next phase after the decision.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the defender scans the opponent before the contest.
Whether the defender recognises uncontested marking opportunities.
Whether risky mark attempts are made under heavy pressure.
Whether unnecessary spoils surrender possession.
Whether field position influences the decision.
Whether the defender responds after an imperfect execution.

commonErrors.error: Defender spoils every football automatically.
commonErrors.correction: Mark when balanced and clearly in front.

commonErrors.error: Defender attempts to mark while badly out of position.
commonErrors.correction: Prioritise preventing the opponent’s mark.

commonErrors.error: Defender decides before reading the kick.
commonErrors.correction: Assess the flight and pressure as the football travels.

commonErrors.error: Defender ignores field position.
commonErrors.correction: Increase caution when a dropped mark would create a direct scoring chance.

commonErrors.error: Spoil is directed to an opponent.
commonErrors.correction: Identify support and safe space before contact.

commonErrors.error: Defender stops after a dropped mark.
commonErrors.correction: Re-enter the contest immediately.

progressions: Add a second attacker.
Vary scoreboard and time scenarios.
Introduce a goalkeeper or defensive leader’s communication.
Continue into a full transition phase.
Use live kicks from moving players.
regressions: Tell the defender the expected pressure level.
Use only two clear scenarios: uncontested mark or obvious spoil.
Pause before the contest and ask the defender to state the decision.
successIndicators: Recognise when a mark is available.
Account for field position and risk.
Execute the chosen action and complete the next phase.
matchApplication: Effective defenders do not spoil automatically. Intercept marks create possession and counterattack, while well-timed spoils prevent dangerous opposition marks. The decision must account for pressure, balance, field position and support.

title: Spoiling Fundamentals Assessment
primarySkill: Assessing complete fundamental spoiling and aerial-defence capability.
objective: Assess each player’s ability to apply the complete fundamental aerial-defence sequence from starting position through to spoil execution and ground-level recovery.
groundSize: One-third of an oval divided into five assessment stations.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Create five assessment stations.
Station 1 assesses balanced starting position and goal-side alignment.
Station 2 assesses controlled approach and spoil timing.
Station 3 assesses one-handed and two-fisted spoiling technique.
Station 4 assesses directional spoiling and field-position awareness.
Station 5 assesses communication, aerial role selection and ground-level recovery.
Divide players evenly across stations.
Assign a coach or experienced observer to each station.
Use a five-point scoring scale for each assessed behaviour.
Modify contact and jumping volume for younger, returning and Over 35 players.
howTheDrillWorks:
Players begin at their allocated station.
Each player completes three to five assessed repetitions.
At Station 1, the player responds to an opponent’s movement while maintaining vision and goal-side position.
At Station 2, the player approaches a moving aerial contest and attempts a legal spoil.
At Station 3, the player performs near-arm, far-side and emergency double-fist spoils according to the delivery.
At Station 4, the player directs the football towards the boundary, support or a nominated safe zone.
At Station 5, two defenders communicate aerial and ground-level roles before completing the contest and exit.
Coaches record scores for positioning, judgement, legality, execution and recovery.
Players rotate after six to eight minutes.
The assessment ends with individual feedback and one priority development target for each player.
coachingPoints: Assess the complete sequence rather than the spoil in isolation.
Reward correct positioning and decision making even when execution is imperfect.
Penalise illegal contact and unsafe technique.
Judge whether the player selects the correct arm and method.
Assess whether the spoil improves the defensive situation.
Observe the response after the football reaches ground level.
Require clear communication in team-based stations.
Provide one specific development priority rather than excessive feedback.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Starting balance and goal-side alignment.
Ability to see the football and opponent.
Approach speed and control.
Jump and spoil timing.
Hand selection and contact quality.
Legality of bodywork.
Direction and distance of the spoil.
Communication and support.
Landing and ground-level recovery.
Consistency across repeated attempts.

commonErrors.error: Player focuses only on making contact with the football.
