commonErrors.correction: Assess and coach the full sequence from starting position to recovery.

commonErrors.error: Defender approaches too quickly and infringes.
commonErrors.correction: Close fast early, then shorten the final steps.

commonErrors.error: Player uses the preferred arm in every situation.
commonErrors.correction: Match the arm and technique to the football’s position.

commonErrors.error: Spoil prevents the mark but creates greater danger.
commonErrors.correction: Direct the football towards the boundary, support or lower-risk space.

commonErrors.error: Communication is late or absent.
commonErrors.correction: Identify aerial and support roles before the jump.

commonErrors.error: Player stops after the aerial action.
commonErrors.correction: Require a second effort before the repetition is scored complete.

progressions: Convert the final station into a live small-sided game.
Add full match-like contact for appropriate senior groups.
Introduce scoreboard and time scenarios.
Assess players in their normal positional roles.
Repeat the assessment later in the chapter to measure improvement.
regressions: Remove live tackling from the recovery phase.
Provide a demonstration before each assessed repetition.
successIndicators: Execute a legal and technically sound spoil.
Recover immediately after the aerial contest.
matchApplication: The assessment measures whether players can apply the fundamental skills required in genuine Australian football contests. Strong aerial defence depends on starting position, flight judgement, legal bodywork, spoil execution, tactical direction and continued involvement after the ball reaches ground level.
relatedDrills: SP-001 – Balanced Aerial Defence Starting Position

title: Moving Lead Tracking
primarySkill: Tracking a moving opponent while maintaining aerial contest position.
objective: Develop the defender’s ability to track a sustained lead, preserve goal-side position and arrive balanced enough to contest the aerial football legally.
groundSize: One 20 x 8-metre channel per group.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations or several behaviours
setup:
Mark a straight 20-metre leading channel.
Position an attacker and defender together at one end.
Place a feeder 15–20 metres away and slightly inside the channel.
The defender begins half a step goal side and on the attacker’s inside shoulder.
The attacker leads continuously through the channel without changing direction during the introductory phase.
The feeder delivers the football once the lead is established.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacker begins a controlled lead on the feeder’s signal.
The defender reacts and accelerates while maintaining the attacker’s inside shoulder.
The defender keeps vision connected to the feeder and football.
The feeder delivers a high or slightly looping kick into the attacker’s path.
The defender closes the final distance and shortens the last three steps.
The defender attempts to mark or spoil according to position.
Both players react to the football if it reaches ground level.
Players rotate through attacker, defender and feeder roles after four repetitions.
coachingPoints: Begin close enough to respond immediately.
Protect the attacker’s goal-side and corridor-side line.
Accelerate without crossing behind the opponent.
Use peripheral vision to track the football.
Avoid looking continuously at the opponent’s back.
Shorten the final steps before entering contact range.
Arrive beside the opponent rather than through the back.
Complete the contest with a ground-level second effort.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the defender preserves goal-side position.
Whether the defender can track the football while running.
Whether the defender closes the final distance under control.
Whether the defender trails directly behind the attacker.
Whether the contest is legal.
Whether the defender reacts after the aerial action.

commonErrors.error: Defender follows directly behind the attacker.
commonErrors.correction: Move towards the inside shoulder and protect the dangerous side.

commonErrors.error: Defender watches only the opponent.
commonErrors.correction: Check the feeder and track the football through peripheral vision.

commonErrors.error: Defender overruns the contest.
commonErrors.correction: Shorten the final steps as the football descends.

commonErrors.error: Defender reaches and holds while running.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain position with foot speed rather than the hands.

commonErrors.error: Defender slows too early.
commonErrors.correction: Accelerate through the open space before controlling the final approach.

commonErrors.error: Defender stops after the spoil.
commonErrors.correction: Land, locate the football and continue defending.

progressions: Increase the lead speed.
Vary the delivery between short and deep.
Allow the attacker to alter the lead angle.
Add a defensive support player at ground level.
Continue play until one team exits the channel.
regressions: Have the attacker move at three-quarter pace.
Keep the defender beside the attacker at the start.
Stop the drill after the aerial contest.
successIndicators: Track the football during the lead.
matchApplication: The drill replicates defending a forward who leads into space. The defender must match the opponent’s movement, retain access to the football and arrive in a legal position to prevent an uncontested mark.

title: Double-Lead Recovery Defence
primarySkill: Recovering defensive position against a double lead.
objective: Develop the defender’s ability to remain balanced through an opponent’s initial lead, recover on the second movement and re-establish a legal aerial contesting position.
groundSize: One 18 x 12-metre channel per group.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations or several behaviours
setup:
Mark an initial lead gate 5 metres from the starting point.
Mark two secondary lead gates on opposite sides of the channel.
Position the attacker and defender together at the starting cone.
Place the feeder 15 metres away.
The attacker must lead towards the first gate before changing direction towards either secondary gate.
The feeder kicks only after the second lead begins.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacker accelerates towards the first gate.
The defender tracks the first movement without overcommitting.
At the gate, the attacker plants and changes direction towards either secondary gate.
The defender lowers the hips, redirects and attempts to regain the inside shoulder.
The feeder delivers the football towards the attacker’s second lead.
The defender closes under control and contests the aerial football.
Play continues for five seconds if the football reaches ground level.
Players rotate after four repetitions in each role.
coachingPoints: Keep the first movement controlled enough to respond to the second lead.
Avoid turning the hips completely before the attacker commits.
Lower the centre of gravity before changing direction.
Push strongly from the outside foot.
Recover towards the attacker’s dangerous shoulder.
Reconnect vision to the football after the change of direction.
Do not grab the opponent when beaten on the turn.
Arrive balanced enough to mark or spoil.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the defender anticipates and guesses the second lead.
Whether the defender remains balanced at the first gate.
Whether the hips and feet redirect efficiently.
Whether the defender uses the hands to recover illegally.
Whether the football is tracked after the turn.
Whether the defender reaches a legitimate contest.

commonErrors.error: Defender commits fully to the first lead.
commonErrors.correction: Use shorter steps and remain balanced until the attacker changes direction.

commonErrors.error: Defender stands upright during the turn.
commonErrors.correction: Lower the hips and push from the outside foot.

commonErrors.error: Defender grabs the attacker after losing position.
commonErrors.correction: Recover with foot speed and attack the inside shoulder.

commonErrors.error: Defender loses sight of the football.
commonErrors.correction: Reconnect the head and shoulders to the feeder after redirecting.

commonErrors.error: Defender takes several small ineffective steps.
commonErrors.correction: Plant decisively and accelerate out of the turn.

commonErrors.error: Defender arrives too fast and infringes.
commonErrors.correction: Control the final steps before entering the contest.

progressions: Allow the attacker to choose whether to complete the second lead.
Add a third lead option.
Increase the speed and kick distance.
Add a supporting defender who communicates the lead direction.
Continue into a live two-on-two contest.
regressions: Nominate the direction of the second lead.
Reduce the speed of the attacker.
Remove contact from the aerial contest.
successIndicators: Stay balanced through the first lead.
Track the football after changing direction.
matchApplication: Forwards frequently use double leads to make defenders overcommit. A defender who controls the first movement and recovers quickly can remain connected and prevent the second lead from becoming an uncontested marking opportunity.

title: Change-of-Direction Aerial Close
primarySkill: Closing an aerial contest after changing defensive direction.
objective: Develop the defender’s ability to recognise a changed kick direction, redirect immediately and arrive under control at a new aerial contest.
groundSize: A 20 x 20-metre square.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Position a feeder on each side of the square.
Place one attacker in each half of the area.
The defender begins centrally and initially faces one feeder.
The coach nominates which feeder begins with the football.
The first feeder may kick or transfer the football to the opposite feeder.
The defender must react to the actual disposal rather than the initial ball location.
howTheDrillWorks:
The defender begins in a central, open stance.
The first feeder shapes to kick towards the nearby attacker.
The feeder either delivers the kick or handballs across to the second feeder.
If the football changes sides, the defender turns, accelerates and closes towards the opposite attacker.
The active feeder delivers a high football once the defender begins moving.
The defender arrives under control and attempts to mark or spoil.
The inactive attacker becomes a ground-level support player.
Play continues for six seconds.
Players rotate after five repetitions.
coachingPoints: Maintain a stance that permits movement in either direction.
React to the football’s disposal rather than the feeder’s body shape.
Turn the hips before accelerating.
Use an efficient crossover step when greater distance must be covered.
Track the football immediately after changing direction.
Close open space quickly.
Shorten the final approach.
Communicate when changing responsibility.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the defender guesses the initial kick.
Whether the defender can redirect without losing balance.
Whether the head locates the football quickly.
Whether the defender takes an efficient closing line.
Whether the final approach remains controlled.
Whether the defender communicates the changed responsibility.

commonErrors.error: Defender commits before the football is disposed.
commonErrors.correction: Hold a balanced central position and react to the actual disposal.

commonErrors.error: Defender turns with multiple small steps.
commonErrors.correction: Open the hips and use one decisive crossover step.

commonErrors.error: Defender runs without finding the football.
commonErrors.correction: Locate the flight immediately after changing direction.

commonErrors.error: Defender takes a curved closing line.
commonErrors.correction: Accelerate directly towards the new drop zone.

commonErrors.error: Defender crashes into the contest.
commonErrors.correction: Shorten the final steps and arrive beside the opponent.

commonErrors.error: Defender remains silent during the transfer.
commonErrors.correction: Call the change and identify the new contest.

progressions: Add a third feeder.
Allow both attackers to move simultaneously.
Begin with live possession movement between feeders.
Add a second defender and require role transfer.
Continue into a defensive exit after the spoil.
regressions: Announce the transfer before it occurs.
Stop after the defender reaches the contest.
successIndicators: Redirect immediately when the football changes sides.
matchApplication: Defenders must frequently change direction when the opposition switches play, handballs through traffic or alters the intended forward entry. Immediate recognition and efficient movement can prevent the new target from receiving an uncontested mark.
relatedDrills: SP-001 – Balanced Aerial Defence Starting Position

title: Backward-to-Forward Contest Transition
primarySkill: Transitioning from backward defensive movement into a forward aerial contest.
objective: Teach defenders to move backwards while tracking a deep football, then plant, drive forward and attack a shorter aerial contest without losing balance.
groundSize: A 22 x 12-metre channel.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Mark a deep target zone and a short target zone within the channel.
Position the defender centrally between the zones.
Place one attacker in each target zone.
The feeder begins 15–20 metres in front of the defender.
The feeder initially shapes to kick deep.
The defender must move backwards before the final target is revealed.
howTheDrillWorks:
The feeder shapes to deliver towards the deep attacker.
The defender opens the hips and moves backwards using drop steps.
The feeder either kicks deep or delivers a shorter floating ball to the front attacker.
If the short kick is used, the defender plants, changes direction and drives forward.
The defender attacks the football at its highest safe point.
The defender marks or spoils according to pressure.
The non-target attacker becomes a support player.
Play continues until possession is secured or the football leaves the channel.
Players rotate after five repetitions.
coachingPoints: Avoid upright backpedalling.
Keep the body half-open while moving backwards.
Maintain visual connection to the football.
Plant strongly before driving forward.
Take the shortest line to the new drop point.
Attack the football rather than waiting underneath it.
Decide early whether the ball can be intercepted.
Control the final approach into contact.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the defender moves backwards safely.
Whether the defender maintains vision of both targets.
Whether the change from backward to forward movement is decisive.
Whether the defender attacks the football.
Whether the defender makes the correct mark-or-spoil decision.
Whether momentum remains controlled at the contest.

commonErrors.error: Defender backpedals upright.
commonErrors.correction: Open the hips and use athletic drop steps.

commonErrors.error: Defender takes too long to reverse direction.
commonErrors.correction: Plant the outside foot and drive immediately towards the short target.

commonErrors.error: Defender waits for the football to arrive.
commonErrors.correction: Attack through the drop point.

commonErrors.error: Defender loses sight of the short attacker.
commonErrors.correction: Scan both targets while maintaining ball vision.

commonErrors.error: Defender spoils an uncontested football.
commonErrors.correction: Recognise front position and complete the intercept mark.

commonErrors.error: Defender overruns the short contest.
commonErrors.correction: Shorten the final steps before reaching the opponent.

progressions: Allow both attackers to lead.
Increase the distance between target zones.
Add a second defender and require communication.
Use live ball movement before the kick.
Continue into a transition attack after an intercept.
regressions: Announce the target zone before the kick.
Practise the movement pattern without a football.
matchApplication: Defenders often retreat to protect deep space before an opposition player lowers the eyes and kicks short. The ability to stop, drive forward and attack the shorter ball creates intercept opportunities and prevents easy possession in front of the defensive line.

title: Lateral Crossover Spoil
primarySkill: Moving laterally into an aerial contest using efficient crossover footwork.
objective: Develop the defender’s ability to cover lateral space quickly and arrive beside an opponent with sufficient balance to execute a clean spoil.
groundSize: A 15 x 15-metre square.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations or several behaviours
setup:
Mark one contest zone on each side of the square.
Position the defender in the centre.
Place an attacker in each contest zone.
The feeder stands directly in front of the defender.
The feeder may deliver to either attacker.
The defender must move laterally rather than retreating deeply.
howTheDrillWorks:
The defender begins in a balanced central stance.
The feeder delivers a high football towards either lateral contest zone.
The defender pushes from the opposite foot and uses crossover steps to cover the space.
As the defender approaches the attacker, the feet return to a balanced running pattern.
The defender closes beside the opponent.
The defender selects the near-side arm and attempts to spoil away from the centre.
The defender lands and recovers towards the central side.
Players rotate after six repetitions.
coachingPoints: Push strongly from the foot opposite the movement direction.
Use crossover steps only while covering open space.
Return to shorter balanced steps near the contest.
Keep the head steady and track the football.
Avoid crossing the legs during the final contact phase.
Arrive on the opponent’s central shoulder where possible.
Use the arm nearest the football.
Direct the spoil towards the outside of the square.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the first movement is explosive.
Whether crossover footwork is efficient.
Whether the defender regains balance before contact.
Whether the football remains in vision.
Whether the correct shoulder and arm are used.
Whether the defender recovers towards central danger.

commonErrors.error: Defender shuffles slowly across open space.
commonErrors.correction: Use a strong crossover step to cover distance.

commonErrors.error: Defender continues crossing the feet into contact.
commonErrors.correction: Return to shorter balanced steps before the contest.

commonErrors.error: Defender reaches across the opponent.
commonErrors.correction: Arrive beside the target and use the near-side arm.

commonErrors.error: Defender drifts behind the attacker.
commonErrors.correction: Attack the central shoulder and protect inside space.

commonErrors.error: Spoil is directed back into the middle.
commonErrors.correction: Angle the fist and follow-through towards the outside.

commonErrors.error: Defender lands and moves away from danger.
commonErrors.correction: Recover immediately towards the central side.

progressions: Allow both attackers to move.
Increase the width of the area.
Add a supporting attacker in the central zone.
Require an immediate defensive exit after the spoil.
Begin the defender from a moving position.
successIndicators: Direct the spoil away from central danger.
matchApplication: Lateral aerial movement is required when defenders cover across from a teammate, protect the weak side or respond to a kick that changes angle. Efficient crossover footwork helps the defender reach the contest without arriving uncontrolled.

title: Help-Side Closing Angle
primarySkill: Closing an aerial contest from a help-side angle.
objective: Teach a supporting defender to close from the help side, avoid interfering with the primary defender and influence the aerial contest towards safety.
groundSize: A 22 x 18-metre area.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Position one attacker and one primary defender in the central contest area.
Place a help-side defender 8–10 metres away on the central or goal side.
A feeder stands 18 metres from the contest.
Mark a safe spoil zone towards the boundary.
The primary defender begins in close checking position.
The help-side defender must decide whether to fly or protect the ground.
howTheDrillWorks:
The feeder delivers a high football towards the attacker.
The primary defender tracks the opponent and contests if able.
The help-side defender reads the flight and communicates their approach.
If the help-side defender has the strongest line, they call and attack the football.
The primary defender remains grounded or applies body pressure without blocking the teammate.
The aerial defender attempts to mark or spoil towards the safe zone.
The grounded defender protects the front and central ground ball.
Play continues until the defensive team exits through a gate or the attackers regain possession.
Roles rotate after four contests.
coachingPoints: Approach from a line that allows clear access to the football.
Communicate before crossing a teammate’s path.
Do not fly if the primary defender already has control of the contest.
The player with the best view and momentum should attack the football.
Avoid arriving through the opponent’s front.
Direct the spoil towards the boundary or defensive support.
The non-flying defender must protect the ground.
Remain connected through the exit phase.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the help-side defender reads the contest early.
Whether communication occurs before the jump.
Whether the closing angle is safe and legal.
Whether defenders collide or spoil each other.
Whether one defender remains grounded.
Whether the defensive pair connects after the spoil.

commonErrors.error: Help-side defender arrives without communicating.
commonErrors.correction: Call early before entering the primary defender’s space.

commonErrors.error: Both defenders fly.
commonErrors.correction: The defender with the weaker line remains grounded and protects the front.

commonErrors.error: Help defender approaches through the attacker’s front.
commonErrors.correction: Adjust the angle to attack the football from the side.

commonErrors.error: Primary defender blocks the teammate’s run.
commonErrors.correction: Release the aerial role and shift immediately to ground coverage.

commonErrors.error: Spoil falls into central danger.
commonErrors.correction: Use the approach angle and follow-through to direct it outside.

commonErrors.error: Defenders separate after the contest.
commonErrors.correction: Recover together and provide an immediate exit option.

progressions: Add a second attacker at ground level.
Begin from live ball movement.
Vary which defender starts in primary position.
Add a third defender who protects behind the contest.
Continue into a full defensive transition.
regressions: Nominate the help-side defender as the aerial contestant.
Pause before the jump to confirm roles.
successIndicators: Exit the contest as a connected defensive unit.
matchApplication: Help-side defenders regularly leave their direct opponent to support a teammate in an aerial contest. Correct timing, communication and approach angle allow the defence to create an extra number without exposing the dangerous ground ball.

title: Recovery Sprint to Aerial Contest
primarySkill: Recovering at speed to contest an aerial football after being caught out of position.
objective: Develop the defender’s ability to recover from a positional disadvantage, take an efficient pursuit line and reach the aerial contest without infringing.
groundSize: A 25 x 10-metre recovery channel.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations or several behaviours
setup:
Position the attacker 5 metres ahead of the defender.
Place the feeder 20–25 metres from the target area.
Mark two recovery gates that create different pursuit lines.
The defender begins slightly out of position following a simulated turnover.
The feeder delivers once the attacker begins leading.
Recovery distances should be adjusted for age and conditioning level.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach calls a recovery gate.
The defender turns and sprints through the nominated gate.
The attacker leads towards the target zone.
The feeder delivers a high football into the attacker’s path.
The defender takes the shortest legal line to the contest.
The defender decelerates before contact and attempts a rear or side spoil.
If unable to reach the football, the defender applies immediate ground-level pressure.
Play continues for six seconds.
Players rotate after four repetitions.
coachingPoints: Turn and accelerate immediately after recognising danger.
Pursue the drop zone rather than the opponent’s exact footsteps.
Use the kick’s hang time to reduce the separation.
Avoid reaching or holding while sprinting.
Shorten the final steps before entering the opponent’s space.
Spoil over or beside the shoulder without pushing in the back.
If the aerial contest cannot be reached, prepare for the ground ball.
Maintain effort through the entire phase.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the defender reacts immediately.
Whether the pursuit line is efficient.
Whether the defender watches the football during recovery.
Whether the defender grabs or pushes the opponent.
Whether final deceleration occurs.
Whether the defender continues competing when unable to spoil.

commonErrors.error: Defender follows directly behind the attacker.
commonErrors.correction: Run towards the expected drop zone and inside shoulder.

commonErrors.error: Defender reaches and holds while recovering.
commonErrors.correction: Keep the arms free and rely on sprint speed.

commonErrors.error: Defender looks only at the attacker.
commonErrors.correction: Track the football’s flight during the pursuit.

commonErrors.error: Defender arrives at full speed and infringes.
commonErrors.correction: Shorten the final steps and enter beside the opponent.

commonErrors.error: Defender gives up when unable to spoil.
commonErrors.correction: Transition immediately into ground-level pressure.

commonErrors.error: Defender takes a wide recovery line.
commonErrors.correction: Identify the shortest legal path to the contest.

progressions: Increase the starting separation.
Allow the attacker to change the lead angle.
Add a second attacker for ground-level support.
Begin from a live turnover.
Require a defensive exit after regaining possession.
successIndicators: React immediately to the recovery cue.
Spoil or apply effective ground-level pressure.
matchApplication: Defenders are sometimes beaten by a turnover, poor starting position or unexpected forward movement. Strong recovery running can still prevent a mark, reduce the quality of the opponent’s possession or force the next contest.

title: Turn-and-Track Deep Ball
primarySkill: Turning and tracking a football delivered over the defender’s head.
objective: Teach defenders to turn efficiently, locate a deep football and recover towards the drop zone without losing awareness of the opponent.
groundSize: A 30 x 12-metre deep channel.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations or several behaviours
setup:
Position the defender facing the feeder.
Place the attacker one metre behind and to either side of the defender.
The feeder stands 15–20 metres away.
Mark a deep drop zone 15 metres behind the defender.
The feeder delivers a long football over the pair.
The attacker initially runs on a straight line.
howTheDrillWorks:
The feeder begins the kicking action.
The defender reads the trajectory and turns towards the side that provides the clearest path.
The defender accelerates towards the deep drop zone.
While running, the defender relocates the football over the shoulder.
The attacker attempts to reach front position.
The defender protects the direct line to the drop zone.
The defender marks, spoils or shepherds the football safely through according to position.
Both players react if the football remains in play.
Players rotate after five repetitions.
coachingPoints: Turn in the direction that keeps the football accessible to vision.
Avoid spinning without knowing the opponent’s location.
Accelerate immediately after the turn.
Use controlled head checks rather than running backwards.
Run towards the drop zone, not directly towards the opponent.
Establish front or side position before the football descends.
Avoid early body contact while the football is distant.
Decide whether to mark, spoil or allow the ball to carry safely.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the defender selects an efficient turn direction.
How quickly the football is relocated.
Whether the defender runs to the drop zone.
Whether the opponent gains easy front position.
Whether body contact occurs too early.
Whether the final decision suits the football’s flight.

commonErrors.error: Defender backpedals instead of turning.
commonErrors.correction: Open the hips and sprint towards the deep drop zone.

commonErrors.error: Defender turns away and cannot relocate the football.
commonErrors.correction: Turn through the side that maintains visual access to the flight.

commonErrors.error: Defender runs towards the attacker rather than the ball.
commonErrors.correction: Target the drop zone and protect the direct line.

commonErrors.error: Defender initiates contact while the football is distant.
commonErrors.correction: Establish running position before applying legal body pressure.

commonErrors.error: Defender moves underneath the football.
commonErrors.correction: Remain slightly goal side and judge the carry.

commonErrors.error: Defender spoils a ball that will carry safely through.
commonErrors.correction: Assess whether intervention is required before committing.

progressions: Allow the attacker to change the running line.
Vary the depth and angle of the kick.
Add a second defender providing cover.
Introduce a scoring line behind the drop zone.
Continue into a live defensive exit.
regressions: Allow the defender to begin side-on.
matchApplication: Deep kicks over the defensive line require defenders to turn, locate the football and protect space towards goal. Efficient tracking reduces panic, prevents illegal contact and improves the chance of marking, spoiling or safely seeing the ball through.
relatedDrills: SP-027 – Recovery Sprint to Aerial Contest

title: Moving Spoil to Defensive Exit
primarySkill: Linking a moving aerial spoil with an organised defensive exit.
objective: Develop the defensive unit’s ability to direct a moving spoil towards support, win the ground-level possession and exit the contest area with control.
groundSize: A 30 x 20-metre area with two defensive exit gates.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Create teams of three defenders and three attackers.
Position one attacker and defender in the aerial starting contest.
Place the remaining players in ground-level support positions.
A feeder stands 20 metres away.
Mark two exit gates on the boundary sides.
Mark a central danger corridor that defenders should avoid when exiting.
howTheDrillWorks:
The aerial attacker leads across the area.
The aerial defender tracks the lead and communicates the intended spoil side.
The feeder delivers a high football.
The defender attempts to direct the spoil towards a supporting teammate.
Ground-level players compete for possession.
If the defenders win the football, they attempt to complete one disposal before exiting through either boundary gate.
If the attackers win possession, they attempt to carry or handball through the central danger corridor.
The phase continues for a maximum of twelve seconds.
The defenders receive three points for a directed spoil followed by a clean exit.
Roles rotate after each phase.
coachingPoints: Identify the preferred spoil side before jumping.
Ground-level defenders should move as the aerial contest develops.
Direct the football towards numbers rather than empty space alone.
Communicate who will gather and who will protect.
Use the first possession to escape pressure.
Avoid exiting through the central danger corridor unless clearly open.
Maintain width and separation between supporting defenders.
Reapply pressure immediately if the spoil is lost.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the aerial defender scans support.
Whether ground-level defenders anticipate the spoil.
Whether the football is directed towards defensive numbers.
Whether gathering and protection roles are clear.
Whether the exit uses safe width.
Whether defenders react quickly when possession is lost.

commonErrors.error: Supporting defenders wait until the ball is spoiled.
commonErrors.correction: Move towards the expected drop area before contact.

commonErrors.error: Spoil is directed without considering teammate position.
commonErrors.correction: Scan and communicate the preferred side early.

commonErrors.error: Two defenders gather and leave no protection.
commonErrors.correction: Nominate one gatherer and one protecting player.

commonErrors.error: Exit disposal returns through central congestion.
commonErrors.correction: Use boundary width unless the corridor is clearly available.

commonErrors.error: Defender admires the spoil.
commonErrors.correction: Land and join the next phase immediately.

commonErrors.error: Defensive shape collapses after a turnover.
commonErrors.correction: Apply immediate pressure and protect the central corridor.

progressions: Add another player to each team.
Begin from live ball movement.
Require two disposals before exiting.
Allow the feeder to join the attacking team.
Expand into a defensive 50 exit scenario.
regressions: Use two defenders against one attacker.
Stop after the first clean defensive possession.
matchApplication: An effective spoil should improve the defensive team’s position rather than simply prevent a mark. Connecting the aerial contest with ground-level support and a controlled exit turns defence into possession and transition.
relatedDrills: SP-027 – Recovery Sprint to Aerial Contest

title: Aerial Defence Movement Assessment Circuit
primarySkill: Assessing movement into and out of aerial defensive contests.
objective: Assess each player’s ability to move efficiently across varied aerial-defence situations while maintaining positioning, legality, decision quality and recovery effort.
groundSize: One-third to one-half of an oval divided into five stations.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Station 1 assesses moving lead tracking.
Station 2 assesses double-lead and change-of-direction recovery.
Station 3 assesses lateral crossover and help-side closing.
Station 4 assesses recovery sprint and deep-ball tracking.
Station 5 assesses a directed spoil followed by a defensive exit.
Divide players evenly across stations.
Assign a coach or experienced observer to each station.
Use a five-point scale for movement efficiency, aerial execution and recovery.
Adjust sprint distance and contact for age, injury history and training load.
howTheDrillWorks:
Players begin at their assigned station.
Each player completes three to five repetitions before rotating.
At Station 1, the defender tracks a straight lead and contests the aerial football.
At Station 2, the defender responds to a double lead or redirected kick.
At Station 3, the defender covers laterally or closes from the help side.
At Station 4, the defender recovers from behind or tracks a deep ball over the defensive line.
At Station 5, the defender directs a spoil towards support and contributes to the exit.
Coaches record movement, positioning, legality, decision making and second effort.
Players receive one immediate technical correction at each station.
The assessment concludes with an individual movement priority for each defender.
coachingPoints: Assess movement before, during and after the aerial contest.
Reward efficient lines rather than effort alone.
Observe whether the football remains in vision.
Check that speed is reduced before contact.
Assess the defender’s ability to use both sides of the body.
Penalise holding, pushing and uncontrolled collisions.
Judge whether the movement creates a better defensive outcome.
Require every repetition to finish with a recovery action.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Initial reaction speed.
Footwork and change-of-direction efficiency.
Pursuit and closing angles.
Football tracking during movement.
Balance entering the contest.
Legality of body position and spoil execution.
Decision quality.
Ground-level recovery.
Communication with supporting defenders.
Consistency under fatigue.

commonErrors.error: Player runs hard but takes an inefficient line.
commonErrors.correction: Target the drop zone and protect dangerous space.

commonErrors.error: Defender loses sight of the football while moving.
commonErrors.correction: Use an open body position and controlled head checks.

commonErrors.error: Player arrives too quickly to contest legally.
commonErrors.correction: Shorten the final steps and lower the centre of gravity.

commonErrors.error: Defender uses the same turn or arm on both sides.
commonErrors.correction: Develop movement and spoil execution in both directions.

commonErrors.error: Player treats the aerial action as the end of the repetition.
commonErrors.correction: Require a ground-level recovery or exit before scoring completion.

commonErrors.error: Technique deteriorates under fatigue.
commonErrors.correction: Increase recovery and restore movement quality before continuing.

progressions: Add live opposition decisions at every station.
Combine stations into continuous movement sequences.
Introduce scoreboard and field-position consequences.
Assess players in their normal match roles.
Finish with a conditioned small-sided aerial-defence game.
successIndicators: Track moving opponents without losing position.
Connect the aerial contest with defensive support and exit.
matchApplication: Aerial defence requires repeated movement across leads, changing kick directions, deep space and support situations. This assessment identifies whether defenders can reach contests efficiently and still execute the technical and tactical actions required to complete the defensive phase.
relatedDrills: SP-027 – Recovery Sprint to Aerial Contest
SP-029 – Moving Spoil to Defensive Exit

title: Mirror Lead Aerial Defence
primarySkill: Mirroring an opponent’s lead while preserving aerial contest position.
objective: Develop the defender’s ability to react to an opponent’s unrestricted lead, remain connected through multiple changes of pace and arrive in a legal aerial contesting position.
groundSize: One 20 x 12-metre channel per group.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations or several behaviours
setup:
Mark a rectangular leading channel.
Position an attacker and defender together at one end.
Place a feeder 15–20 metres away.
The attacker may lead forwards, laterally or on an angle but must remain inside the channel.
The defender begins half a step goal side.
The feeder delivers only after the attacker has completed at least one change of pace or direction.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacker begins moving on the feeder’s signal.
The defender mirrors the movement while remaining goal side and close enough to influence.
The attacker may accelerate, decelerate or change direction.
The defender adjusts without reaching or holding.
The feeder delivers a high football once separation or a clear contest line develops.
The defender closes under control and attempts to mark or spoil.
If the football reaches ground level, both players compete for five seconds.
Players rotate through attacker, defender and feeder roles after four repetitions.
coachingPoints: React to the attacker rather than guessing the lead.
Maintain a position from which the football remains visible.
Use short adjustment steps when the attacker slows.
Accelerate decisively when the opponent commits to a lead.
Avoid crossing directly behind the attacker.
Close towards the dangerous shoulder.
Reduce speed before entering contact range.
Finish with an immediate second effort.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the defender remains balanced during changes of pace.
Whether goal-side position is preserved.
Whether the defender watches both the football and opponent.
Whether illegal holding occurs when separation develops.
Whether the defender arrives beside rather than behind.
Whether the defender reacts after the aerial contest.

commonErrors.error: Defender anticipates the lead and moves early.
commonErrors.correction: Hold balance and react to the attacker’s actual movement.

commonErrors.error: Defender stands too far away to influence.
commonErrors.correction: Begin within an arm’s length and remain connected.

commonErrors.error: Defender reaches when the attacker accelerates.
commonErrors.correction: Use foot speed and recover towards the dangerous shoulder.

commonErrors.error: Defender crosses behind the opponent.
commonErrors.correction: Protect the inside and goal-side line.

commonErrors.error: Defender enters the contest at full speed.
commonErrors.correction: Shorten the final steps before contact range.

commonErrors.error: Defender stops after the spoil.
commonErrors.correction: Land, locate the football and continue defending.

progressions: Allow the attacker to use unlimited direction changes.
Add a second feeder to vary the kick angle.
Introduce a supporting attacker at ground level.
Require the defender to direct the spoil towards a nominated side.
Continue until one team exits the channel.
regressions: Restrict the attacker to two movement options.
successIndicators: Adjust to changes of speed and direction.
Arrive balanced at the aerial contest.
Execute a legal mark or spoil.
matchApplication: Forwards rarely lead in perfectly straight lines. Defenders must mirror changes of pace and direction while protecting dangerous space and remaining capable of contesting the eventual kick.
relatedDrills: SP-027 – Recovery Sprint to Aerial Contest
SP-030 – Aerial Defence Movement Assessment Circuit

title: Arc Lead Contest
primarySkill: Defending an opponent leading on a curved arc.
objective: Teach defenders to track a curved lead, protect the inside line and arrive on the correct shoulder to contest the aerial football.
groundSize: One 20 x 15-metre curved leading lane per group.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations or several behaviours
setup:
Use flat markers to create a curved leading lane.
Position an attacker and defender at the beginning of the arc.
Place a feeder 15–18 metres inside the curve.
The defender begins on the inside and goal-side shoulder.
The attacker follows the curved lane during the first phase.
The feeder delivers into the final third of the arc.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacker accelerates along the curved lead.
The defender tracks from the inside shoulder.
The defender avoids following the attacker’s exact outside path.
The feeder delivers a high football towards the end of the lead.
The defender closes the angle between the football and attacker.
The defender attempts to mark or spoil towards the outside of the arc.
Both players recover towards the football.
Players rotate after four repetitions on each side.
coachingPoints: Protect the shorter inside route.
Avoid being carried towards the outside of the arc.
Keep the hips directed towards the likely drop point.
Use the curve to close space rather than matching every step.
Track the football once the feeder disposes.
Arrive on the attacker’s inside shoulder.
Use the near-side arm where possible.
Direct the spoil away from central space.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the defender protects the inside path.
Whether the defender follows too wide.
Whether the football is tracked early.
Whether the defender arrives on the correct shoulder.
Whether the spoil is directed away from danger.
Whether the defender maintains balance on the curved run.

commonErrors.error: Defender follows the attacker’s outside path.
commonErrors.correction: Take the shorter inside line towards the drop zone.

commonErrors.error: Defender turns the shoulders away from the football.
commonErrors.correction: Keep the upper body open to the feeder.

commonErrors.error: Defender cuts across the attacker’s legs.
commonErrors.correction: Close beside the opponent without entering their running path.

commonErrors.error: Defender arrives behind the contest.
commonErrors.correction: Accelerate towards the inside shoulder earlier.

commonErrors.error: Spoil returns to central space.
commonErrors.correction: Use the near-side arm and direct the follow-through outside.

commonErrors.error: Defender loses balance on the arc.
commonErrors.correction: Shorten steps and keep the hips underneath the body.

progressions: Allow the attacker to leave the marked arc.
Reverse the direction of the lead without warning.
Add a second attacker in central space.
Add a supporting defender who communicates the safe side.
Continue into a ground-level contest and exit.
regressions: Reduce the speed of the lead.
successIndicators: Maintain connection through the curved lead.
Direct the football away from central danger.
matchApplication: Forwards often curve their leads to open kicking angles or create separation. Defenders who protect the shorter inside route can reduce space and arrive in a stronger aerial position.

title: Cross-Leading Traffic Defence
primarySkill: Maintaining aerial defensive position through crossing leads and player traffic.
objective: Develop defenders’ ability to track direct opponents through crossing leads, communicate potential switches and avoid losing aerial responsibility in traffic.
groundSize: A 22 x 18-metre area.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Position two attackers on opposite sides of the area.
Match each attacker with a defender.
Place a feeder 18–20 metres in front.
Attackers must cross paths before leading into separate aerial zones.
Defenders may retain their opponent or call a switch.
Mark two target zones for the feeder.
howTheDrillWorks:
Both attackers begin their leads simultaneously.
The attackers cross in the centre before separating.
Defenders communicate whether to retain or switch opponents.
The feeder delivers to either target zone.
The responsible defender closes to the aerial contest.
The second defender protects the dangerous ground-level space.
Play continues for eight seconds.
The defensive team scores for a clear role call followed by a mark, spoil or controlled exit.
The attacking team scores for an uncontested mark or defensive communication error.
Players rotate after four phases.
coachingPoints: Scan both attackers before the crossing point.
Communicate early and use agreed switch language.
Do not collide with a teammate while chasing an opponent.
Retain the direct opponent when a switch creates greater danger.
Transfer responsibility only when both defenders acknowledge.
The non-contesting defender must protect the ground.
Continue tracking the football during the crossing movement.
Recover goal side if the initial role decision fails.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether defenders scan before the leads cross.
Whether communication occurs early enough.
Whether both defenders understand the role decision.
Whether defenders collide or become screened.
Whether the correct defender contests the football.
Whether ground-level space is protected.

commonErrors.error: Defenders communicate after the crossing point.
commonErrors.correction: Call the retain or switch decision before traffic develops.

commonErrors.error: Both defenders follow the same attacker.
commonErrors.correction: Acknowledge individual responsibility clearly.

commonErrors.error: Defender watches only the direct opponent.
commonErrors.correction: Scan the second attacker and teammate before the crossing movement.

commonErrors.error: Defenders collide while navigating traffic.
commonErrors.correction: Adjust running lines and communicate who passes in front.

commonErrors.error: Both defenders fly for the football.
commonErrors.correction: Send the best-positioned defender aerially and keep the other grounded.

commonErrors.error: Defender gives up after losing the match-up.
commonErrors.correction: Recover immediately to goal-side support.

progressions: Add a third attacker and defender.
Allow attackers to fake the crossing movement.
Begin from live handball movement.
Permit the feeder to delay the kick.
Continue into a full defensive exit.
regressions: Predetermine whether defenders retain or switch.
successIndicators: Contest the aerial football with support underneath.
matchApplication: Crossing leads are used to screen defenders and create confusion inside forward 50. Clear communication and disciplined role transfer prevent attackers from becoming free aerial targets.

title: Inside-Out Lead Recovery
primarySkill: Recovering from an inside starting position to defend an opponent leading towards the boundary.
objective: Teach defenders to open from an inside position, recover towards a wide lead and preserve the boundary as the safe defensive side.
groundSize: One 20 x 15-metre boundary-side channel per group.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations or several behaviours
setup:
Mark a boundary line along one side of the channel.
Position the attacker inside the defender at the starting cone.
Place the feeder centrally, 15–18 metres away.
The attacker leads from the inside towards the boundary.
The defender must open the hips and recover to the attacker’s central shoulder.
Mark a safe spoil zone outside the contest.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacker begins an angled lead towards the boundary.
The defender opens the hips and accelerates across the lead.
The defender attempts to reach the attacker’s central shoulder.
The feeder delivers into the wide lead.
The defender closes under control and contests the football.
The defender attempts to spoil towards the boundary safety zone.
If the defensive team wins possession, the defender exits through the boundary gate.
Players rotate after four repetitions on each side.
coachingPoints: Turn the hips early when the wide lead begins.
Run towards the attacker’s central shoulder.
Avoid taking a path that concedes the corridor.
Use the boundary as defensive support.
Track the football after the first three recovery steps.
Arrive beside the opponent.
Direct the spoil outside.
Recover inside after landing.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the defender opens efficiently.
Whether the recovery line protects central space.
Whether the defender reaches the correct shoulder.
Whether the football remains visible.
Whether the spoil reaches the boundary side.
Whether the defender recovers inside after the contest.

commonErrors.error: Defender turns towards the boundary and concedes inside position.
commonErrors.correction: Recover towards the attacker’s central shoulder.

commonErrors.error: Defender takes several small turning steps.
commonErrors.correction: Open the hips decisively and accelerate.

commonErrors.error: Defender watches only the attacker.
commonErrors.correction: Reconnect vision to the feeder after beginning the recovery.

commonErrors.error: Defender approaches from behind.
commonErrors.correction: Cut towards the inside shoulder earlier.

commonErrors.error: Spoil returns into the corridor.
commonErrors.correction: Use the near-side arm and direct the follow-through outside.

commonErrors.error: Defender lands outside the opponent.
commonErrors.correction: Recover immediately towards goal-side and central space.

progressions: Allow the attacker to fake the wide lead and return inside.
Add a central attacking option.
Add a supporting defender.
Begin from live ball movement.
Continue into a two-disposal defensive exit.
regressions: Reduce the angle of the lead.
successIndicators: Direct the football towards the boundary.
matchApplication: Defenders often begin in a central position before an opponent leads wide. The correct recovery line prevents the forward from turning back inside and keeps the aerial contest in a safer boundary-side location.

title: Release-and-Recover Aerial Defence
primarySkill: Releasing from an initial opponent and recovering to a new aerial threat.
objective: Develop the defender’s ability to recognise when an initial opponent is no longer dangerous, release responsibility and close to a more threatening aerial target.
groundSize: A 25 x 22-metre area.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Position two attackers and two defenders across the area.
One attacker begins short and one begins deep.
The feeder starts with the football at the top of the area.
The short attacker may lead away from goal and become a low threat.
The deep attacker may lead into a dangerous aerial zone.
Defenders may transfer responsibility only through clear communication.
howTheDrillWorks:
Both attackers begin moving.
The feeder assesses the movement and prepares to kick.
The defender on the short attacker scans the developing deep threat.
If the short attacker is covered or moving away from danger, the defender may release and provide aerial support.
The second defender communicates whether help is required.
The feeder delivers to either attacker.
Defenders adjust responsibilities and contest the football.
Play continues until the defensive team exits or the attacking team scores through a marked gate.
Points reward correct decisions, not merely successful outcomes.
Players rotate after four phases.
coachingPoints: Assess threat according to field position, ball location and opponent movement.
Do not release an opponent who remains a direct scoring threat.
Communicate before leaving the initial match-up.
The primary defender should call whether aerial help is required.
Take a direct help-side line.
Avoid arriving late and creating unnecessary contact.
Protect the dangerous ground-level space if unable to fly.
Reconnect to an opponent after the aerial phase.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether defenders scan beyond direct opponents.
Whether release decisions reflect genuine danger.
Whether communication precedes the match-up transfer.
Whether the help-side line is efficient.
Whether two defenders crowd the contest.
Whether defenders reconnect after the ball is spoiled.

commonErrors.error: Defender follows a low-threat opponent away from goal.
commonErrors.correction: Scan the dangerous space and release when team structure permits.

commonErrors.error: Defender leaves without communicating.
commonErrors.correction: Call the release and identify the new responsibility.

commonErrors.error: Defender releases too early and leaves a free short target.
commonErrors.correction: Confirm that the initial opponent is covered or moving to low-value space.

commonErrors.error: Help defender arrives through the front of the contest.
commonErrors.correction: Close from the side and preserve a legal line to the football.

commonErrors.error: Both defenders fly.
commonErrors.correction: The weaker line protects the ground.

commonErrors.error: Defender fails to reconnect after the contest.
commonErrors.correction: Identify the nearest dangerous opponent immediately after landing.

progressions: Add a third attacker and defender.
Begin from live possession movement.
Allow attackers to rotate positions.
Introduce scoreboard and time scenarios.
Continue into a full defensive transition.
regressions: Predetermine when the defender should release.
Pause before the kick to discuss the threat.
successIndicators: Identify the most dangerous aerial threat.
Arrive on an effective help-side line.
matchApplication: Team defence requires players to leave low-threat opponents and support dangerous aerial contests. Correct release decisions create intercept and spoiling opportunities without unnecessarily conceding free possession elsewhere.

title: Peel-Off Deep Spoil
primarySkill: Peeling away from a short opponent to defend a deep aerial ball.
objective: Teach defenders to recognise a kick travelling over the initial contest, peel into deep space and prevent the football from reaching a dangerous opponent behind the play.
groundSize: A 30 x 18-metre channel.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Position one short attacker and defender 12 metres from the feeder.
Position a deep attacker 10 metres behind the first contest.
Place a covering defender slightly central of the deep attacker.
The feeder may kick short or over the first contest.
Mark a deep scoring zone behind the second attacker.
Defenders must communicate the peel and cover responsibilities.
howTheDrillWorks:
The short attacker presents towards the feeder.
The feeder may deliver short or kick over the first contest.
If the ball travels deep, the short defender releases and peels towards the second contest.
The covering defender communicates whether they can contest.
The defender with the best line attacks the football.
The second defender protects the front and central ground ball.
The deep attacker attempts to mark or bring the ball to advantage.
Play continues for eight seconds.
The defensive team scores for preventing a deep mark and exiting the area.
Players rotate after four phases.
coachingPoints: Read the kick’s depth immediately.
Do not remain attached to a short opponent when the football has travelled beyond them.
Turn and run towards the deep drop zone.
Communicate who will fly.
Avoid two defenders approaching on the same line.
Protect the front and central side.
Spoil away from the deep scoring zone.
Reconnect to the nearest threat after the contest.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the short defender recognises the deep kick.
How quickly the peel begins.
Whether defenders communicate roles.
Whether the closing lines remain separate.
Whether the spoil clears the scoring zone.
Whether the defensive unit remains connected afterwards.

commonErrors.error: Defender stays with the short opponent after the ball passes.
commonErrors.correction: Release immediately and protect the deeper threat.

commonErrors.error: Peel begins only after the deep attacker is under the ball.
commonErrors.correction: Read the kick’s trajectory at disposal.

commonErrors.error: Both defenders fly from the same line.
commonErrors.correction: Communicate and keep one player grounded.

commonErrors.error: Defender approaches through the deep attacker’s back.
commonErrors.correction: Adjust to a side-on contesting line.

commonErrors.error: Spoil drops into the goal-side space.
commonErrors.correction: Direct the football wider or towards support.

commonErrors.error: Defenders lose short opponents after the contest.
commonErrors.correction: Reconnect immediately once the deep threat is resolved.

progressions: Add a second short attacker.
Allow the feeder to use a short possession before kicking deep.
Add a third defender as goalkeeper.
Continue into a full defensive 50 exit.
Introduce scoreboard and time pressure.
successIndicators: Recognise when the football has travelled beyond the initial contest.
Clear or control the next possession.
matchApplication: When the football travels over an initial leading contest, defenders must release and protect deeper space. Quick peel-off movement prevents forwards behind the play from receiving uncontested marks close to goal.

title: Rotating Match-Up Aerial Coverage
primarySkill: Maintaining aerial coverage while opponents rotate positions.
objective: Develop defenders’ ability to maintain collective aerial coverage when attackers rotate positions and direct match-ups become unclear.
groundSize: A 28 x 22-metre area.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Create teams of three attackers and three defenders.
Position attackers at deep, central and wide starting points.
Defenders begin in a compact triangular shape.
A feeder starts outside the area.
Attackers rotate positions before the kick.
Defenders must decide whether to follow, pass on or zone the movement.
Mark two defensive exit gates.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attackers begin rotating through the three positions.
Defenders communicate responsibility and maintain collective spacing.
The feeder may deliver at any time after the first rotation.
The defender with the strongest line contests the aerial football.
The remaining defenders protect front, central and goal-side space.
If the football reaches ground level, play continues live.
The defensive team attempts to exit through either gate.
The attacking team attempts to retain possession inside the area.
Coaches score communication, spacing and aerial-role selection.
Teams rotate after four possessions.
coachingPoints: Maintain awareness of all three attackers.
Avoid being dragged into excessive direct-opponent chasing.
Communicate each pass-on or retained match-up.
Keep defensive spacing connected.
Identify the most dangerous target as the kick develops.
Send the best-positioned defender aerially.
Protect the front and central ground ball.
Reorganise immediately after the contest.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether defenders scan beyond their direct opponents.
Whether role transfers are communicated.
Whether defensive spacing becomes stretched.
Whether the correct defender contests.
Whether ground-level space is covered.
Whether shape is restored after the contest.

commonErrors.error: Defenders follow every rotation individually.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain team shape and pass opponents on when appropriate.

commonErrors.error: Role transfers occur silently.
commonErrors.correction: Use clear, early communication.

commonErrors.error: Defenders become flat across the field.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain depth and staggered coverage.

commonErrors.error: The deepest attacker becomes unguarded.
commonErrors.correction: Prioritise the most dangerous goal-side threat.

commonErrors.error: All defenders move towards the aerial contest.
commonErrors.correction: Keep coverage underneath and behind the ball.

commonErrors.error: Defensive shape remains disorganised after the spoil.
commonErrors.correction: Re-establish roles immediately.

progressions: Add a fourth attacker and defender.
Begin from live ball movement.
Permit attackers to block or screen legally.
Add scoreboard consequences.
Expand into a full forward-50 team-defence scenario.
regressions: Predetermine whether defenders follow or pass on.
Pause before the kick to check positions.
matchApplication: Forward lines frequently rotate to create mismatches and disrupt defensive communication. Strong team defence requires connected spacing and clear transfer of aerial responsibility rather than six isolated one-on-one match-ups.

title: Wide-to-Corridor Closing Contest
primarySkill: Closing from a wide defensive position into a central aerial contest.
objective: Develop the defender’s ability to leave a wide position, close towards a central aerial threat and contest without exposing the boundary-side opponent unnecessarily.
groundSize: A 30 x 25-metre area.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Mark a central corridor zone and a wide boundary zone.
Position one attacker in each zone.
Match each attacker with a defender.
Place the feeder 20 metres from the central target.
The wide defender may leave their opponent to support the central contest.
The central defender communicates whether help is required.
The wide attacker becomes available if abandoned too early.
howTheDrillWorks:
Both attackers move within their zones.
The feeder prepares to deliver to the central attacker or the wide target.
The wide defender scans the central contest while maintaining awareness of the direct opponent.
If the ball is delivered centrally, the wide defender closes on an angled help-side line.
The central defender either contests or remains grounded according to communication.
If the ball is delivered wide, the wide defender must recover to the direct opponent.

Players rotate after five phases.

Scan the feeder rather than watching only the direct opponent.
Do not leave the wide player before the kick commits centrally.
Close on an angle that protects the corridor.
Communicate which defender will contest.
Avoid arriving through the front of the central opponent.
Direct the spoil towards the wide defensive side.
Recover to the nearest dangerous opponent after the contest.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the wide defender scans centrally.
Whether the release is timed to the actual kick.
Whether the closing line protects the corridor.
Whether the wide attacker is abandoned prematurely.
Whether defenders coordinate the aerial role.
Whether recovery occurs after the contest.

commonErrors.correction: Hold a balanced support position until the ball travels centrally.

commonErrors.error: Defender closes directly through the opponent’s front.

commonErrors.error: Both defenders fly for the central ball.
commonErrors.correction: Communicate and keep the weaker line grounded.

commonErrors.error: Spoil returns to the corridor.
commonErrors.correction: Direct the contact towards the wide defensive side.

commonErrors.error: Defender remains at the contest after the ball moves away.
commonErrors.correction: Reconnect immediately to the nearest dangerous opponent.

Begin from live ball movement.
Allow wide and central attackers to exchange positions.
Add a goalkeeper organising the defence.
Continue into a full transition phase.

Close on a safe, efficient angle.
Avoid conceding an easy wide possession.

title: Repeat Aerial Effort Chain
primarySkill: Completing repeated aerial defensive efforts within one continuous phase.
objective: Develop the defender’s ability to recover from one aerial contest, identify the next threat and complete repeated legal efforts without losing technique or defensive structure.
groundSize: A 30 x 22-metre area containing three contest zones.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Mark three aerial contest zones in a triangular pattern.
Position one attacker in each zone.
Use two defenders who begin in the first zone.
Place a feeder outside each zone with a football.
Coaches control the sequence of deliveries.
Defenders must transition from one contest to the next.
Limit each work period to 25–35 seconds.
howTheDrillWorks:
The first feeder delivers to the opening aerial contest.
One defender contests while the second protects the ground.
Immediately after the outcome, the coach calls the next zone.
Both defenders recover towards the second contest.
Defenders communicate who will fly and who will support.
A second football is delivered before the defenders are fully reset.
The sequence continues into the third zone.
Points are awarded for legal spoils, intercept marks, safe direction and second efforts.
Defenders complete one work period before rotating.
Full recovery is provided between repetitions.
coachingPoints: Recover immediately after each contest.
Communicate roles while moving.
Preserve legal approach technique under fatigue.
Do not allow both defenders to fly.
Read the new football rather than watching the previous result.
Maintain a safe spoil direction.
Use efficient running lines between zones.
Reduce intensity if jumping or contact technique deteriorates.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Speed of recovery between contests.
Quality of communication under fatigue.
Whether one defender remains grounded.
Whether final approach control deteriorates.
Whether spoil technique remains legal.
Whether defenders identify the next threat quickly.
Whether recovery lines remain efficient.
Whether fatigue creates unsafe behaviour.

commonErrors.error: Defenders watch the result of the previous contest.
commonErrors.correction: Turn immediately and identify the next football.

commonErrors.error: Both defenders fly when fatigued.
commonErrors.correction: Re-establish the one-up, one-down rule.

commonErrors.error: Defender approaches the second contest uncontrolled.
commonErrors.correction: Reduce stride length before entering contact range.

commonErrors.error: Communication disappears under fatigue.
commonErrors.correction: Require the aerial role to be called before the ball is delivered.

commonErrors.error: Spoil direction becomes random.
commonErrors.correction: Identify the safe side during the recovery run.

commonErrors.error: Technique deteriorates across repetitions.
commonErrors.correction: Increase recovery or shorten the work period.

Randomise the contest order.
Add ground-level continuation after each spoil.
Introduce a defensive exit after the final contest.
Begin from live opposition ball movement.
successIndicators: Execute legal aerial actions under fatigue.
Complete all phases with safe technique.

SP-029 – Moving Spoil to Defensive Exit

title: Aerial Defence Movement Game

objective: Assess and reinforce the movement skills required to track leads, transfer opponents, support aerial contests and complete defensive exits in a continuous match-like environment.

coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Create an attacking team and defending team of five to ten players each.
Mark one attacking scoring zone and two defensive exit gates.
Place two neutral feeders outside the playing area.
All forward entries must initially be aerial kicks of at least 15 metres.
Attackers may lead, cross, rotate and block legally.
Defenders may retain, switch, peel or provide help-side support.
Adjust contact rules according to age and competition level.
howTheDrillWorks:
Play begins with a neutral feeder or attacking player outside the area.
The attacking team moves to create an aerial target.
The defending team communicates match-ups and aerial coverage.
An aerial kick is delivered into the playing area.
Defenders attempt to mark or spoil towards support or safe width.
If the defenders win possession, they score by moving the football through either exit gate.
If the attackers win possession, they attempt to score through the attacking zone.
After a score, turnover or boundary result, the coach restarts from a different feeder.
The defending team receives bonus points for a directed spoil followed by a controlled exit.
Play is completed in three- to five-minute blocks with coaching between periods.
coachingPoints: Track opponent movement without losing sight of the football.
Communicate retain, switch and help-side decisions.
Protect central and goal-side space.
Send the defender with the best line to the aerial contest.
Keep support underneath the football.
Direct spoils towards defensive numbers or the boundary.
Recover immediately after every contest.
Convert defensive wins into controlled exits.

Whether defenders maintain effective starting positions.
Whether moving opponents are tracked through leads and rotations.
Whether switches and releases are communicated.
Whether aerial support arrives on safe lines.
Whether defenders crowd the contest.
Whether spoils improve the defensive situation.
Whether players recover after aerial efforts.
Whether the defensive team exits with structure.

commonErrors.error: Defenders become absorbed in direct opponents and lose the football.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain an open body position and scan the ball carrier.

commonErrors.error: Match-up changes occur without communication.
commonErrors.correction: Use clear retain, switch and release calls.

commonErrors.error: Multiple defenders fly for the same football.
commonErrors.correction: Send the best line and keep support grounded.

commonErrors.error: Spoils fall into central attacking space.

commonErrors.error: Defenders remain at the contest after the ball moves.
commonErrors.correction: Recover immediately to the next threat.

commonErrors.correction: Use width and support before exiting.

Add scoreboard and time-pressure scenarios.
Require defenders to complete two disposals before exiting.
Introduce repeated forward entries after incomplete exits.
Expand the area and use positional lines.

Execute legal and tactically useful spoils.
Convert defensive possession into structured exits.

title: Shoulder-Pressure Spoil Entry
primarySkill: Entering an aerial contest while absorbing controlled shoulder pressure.
objective: Develop the defender’s ability to maintain balance, protect the line to the football and execute a legal spoil while receiving controlled shoulder-to-shoulder pressure.
groundSize: One 12 x 10-metre contest area per group.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations or several behaviours
setup:
Position an attacker and defender side by side, 6 metres from a marked drop zone.
Place a feeder 10–12 metres in front of the pair.
The defender begins on the goal-side or corridor-side shoulder.
The attacker may apply controlled shoulder pressure while both players move towards the drop zone.
Extended-arm pushes, holding and contact to the back are prohibited.
The feeder delivers a controlled high football once the pair enter the final 3 metres.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacker and defender move together towards the drop zone.
The attacker applies controlled shoulder-to-shoulder pressure.
The defender maintains a strong base and keeps the feet moving.
The feeder delivers the football into the contest.
The defender absorbs the pressure without leaning excessively or extending the arms.
The defender jumps from balance and attempts to spoil the football towards safety.
Both players land and react to the loose football.
Players rotate after four contests on each side.
coachingPoints: Establish shoulder position before heavy pressure develops.
Keep the hips underneath the body.
Maintain foot movement through the contact.
Match the opponent’s force without pushing away.
Keep the eyes on the football.
Jump upwards rather than across the opponent.
Use the arm nearest the football.
Recover immediately after landing.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the defender remains balanced under pressure.
Whether the defender extends an arm into the opponent.
Whether shoulder contact remains legal.
Whether the football stays in vision.
Whether the defender can jump effectively after contact.
Whether the defender completes a second effort.

commonErrors.error: Defender leans heavily into the opponent.
commonErrors.correction: Keep the chest over the hips and maintain foot movement.

commonErrors.error: Defender pushes away with the forearm.
commonErrors.correction: Hold position through the shoulder and body rather than extending the arm.

commonErrors.error: Defender becomes flat-footed.
commonErrors.correction: Use short adjustment steps through the contact.

commonErrors.error: Defender jumps across the opponent.
commonErrors.correction: Jump vertically from a balanced base.

commonErrors.error: Defender loses sight of the football.
commonErrors.correction: Keep the head and near shoulder open to the feeder.

Add ground-level support players.

title: Late Contact Aerial Stability
primarySkill: Maintaining aerial technique when legal body pressure arrives late.
objective: Teach defenders to remain composed and complete the spoiling action when controlled legal contact occurs immediately before take-off.
groundSize: One 10 x 8-metre contest area per group.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations or several behaviours
setup:
Position the defender inside a marked take-off zone.
Place an attacker or pad holder beside the defender.
A feeder stands 8–10 metres away.
The feeder delivers a controlled high football.
The attacker applies a light legal shoulder contact as the defender prepares to jump.
Contact force must remain controlled and age appropriate.
howTheDrillWorks:
The feeder delivers the football towards the defender’s reach.
The defender tracks the flight and establishes a stable take-off position.
The attacker applies a controlled shoulder contact immediately before the defender jumps.
The defender absorbs the contact without stepping across or losing football vision.
The defender jumps and performs a one-handed spoil.
The defender lands with soft knees and regains balance.
The defender then moves towards the football’s landing area.
Players rotate after five repetitions on each side.
coachingPoints: Expect contact without bracing too early.
Keep the feet underneath the body.
Tighten the trunk while keeping the upper body relaxed.
Maintain football vision through the contact.
Do not retaliate or push away.
Complete the arm extension fully.
Land with a wide enough base to regain balance.
Follow the football immediately.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the defender anticipates contact without becoming rigid.
Whether the football remains in vision.
Whether the spoiling arm reaches full extension.
Whether the defender pushes the opponent.
Whether take-off remains safe.
Whether landing balance is maintained.

commonErrors.error: Defender braces too early and becomes stationary.

commonErrors.error: Defender turns towards the opponent.

commonErrors.error: Defender pushes back after contact.
commonErrors.correction: Absorb through the body and continue the football action.

commonErrors.error: Spoiling arm shortens at contact.
commonErrors.correction: Extend fully through the football.

commonErrors.error: Defender jumps from crossed feet.

title: Front-Position Pressure Hold
primarySkill: Protecting front position while an opponent applies pressure from behind.

coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations or several behaviours
setup:
Position the defender one metre in front of the attacker.
Mark a 4-metre drop zone.
Place the feeder 12 metres away.
The attacker may apply controlled pressure from behind while attempting to reach the football.
Pushing in the back, holding and forceful contact are prohibited.
The defender must decide whether to mark, spoil or bring the football safely to ground.
howTheDrillWorks:
The feeder delivers a high football towards the marked drop zone.
The defender tracks backwards or laterally while protecting front position.
The attacker applies controlled pressure from behind or beside the defender.
The defender keeps the feet moving and avoids backing directly into the opponent.
The defender judges whether the football can be marked safely.
If the mark is not secure, the defender spoils laterally or over the boundary side.
Both players recover to the ground-level contest.
Players rotate after five repetitions.

Keep a balanced base while moving backwards.
Use body position rather than extended arms.
Avoid backing underneath the football.
Feel the opponent without turning away from the flight.
Mark only when balance and control are present.
Spoil away from central danger when under heavy pressure.
Land and protect the next possession.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the defender maintains front position.
Whether the defender backs recklessly into the opponent.
Whether illegal holding occurs.
Whether the defender judges the football accurately.
Whether the mark-or-spoil decision reflects pressure.
Whether the defender completes the ground-level phase.
