title: Opposed High-Ball Decision Contest
primarySkill: Making an aerial defensive decision under full one-on-one pressure.

groundSize: One 15 x 12-metre contest area per group.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Position one attacker and defender inside the contest area.
Place the feeder 15–20 metres away.
Vary the defender’s starting position between front, side and rear.
Mark a boundary-side safe zone and a central danger zone.
The feeder varies the height, depth and direction of the delivery.
Contact must remain legal and appropriate for the playing group.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach nominates the starting relationship without specifying the required action.
The feeder delivers a high football into the contest.
The defender assesses the flight, balance and opponent’s position.
The defender chooses to mark, one-hand spoil, two-fist spoil or bring the football safely to ground.
The attacker competes genuinely for the mark.

The defender scores for correct decision quality, legal execution and safe direction.

Players rotate after five contests.

Use the starting position to inform the decision.
Mark when clearly balanced and in control.
Spoil when disadvantaged or under significant pressure.

Direct the football away from central danger.
Avoid conceding free kicks through panic contact.
Complete the next phase.

Whether the defender recognises the starting advantage or disadvantage.
Whether the selected action suits the football’s flight.

title: Pack-Entry Spoil Lane

Position two attackers and one primary defender inside the drop zone.

The feeder delivers a high football towards the pack.

Approach only through a clear and legal lane.
Communicate loudly before entering.
Avoid jumping into an opponent’s exposed front.
Do not spoil a teammate who already controls the football.
Remain grounded when the entry lane is unsafe.
Protect the front and central ground ball.
Recover and reorganise after the contest.

Whether the support defender scans before entering.
Whether the selected lane is safe.
Whether communication occurs early.
Whether teammates collide.
Whether front-on contact is avoided.

Whether the ground ball is protected.
Whether the defence reorganises afterwards.

Continue into a defensive exit.

Do not allow fatigue to produce panic contact.
Shorten the final steps.
Keep the eyes on the football.

Land with control.
Prioritise technique quality over exhaustion.

Whether the defender takes an efficient recovery line.

Whether contact remains legal.
Whether spoil timing deteriorates.

howTheDrillWorks:
The feeder delivers a high wet football into the contest.
The defender assesses whether a mark can be secured safely.

The defender lands with reduced stride length and maintains balance.
The defensive team attempts to gather and exit through a boundary gate.
The attacking team attempts to win possession inside the danger zone.
Play continues for eight seconds.
Roles rotate after four repetitions.

Allow additional space for the ball’s skid and carry.
Avoid low-percentage overhead marking attempts under pressure.
Use a firm fist rather than an open-handed slap.

Keep the feet underneath the body on landing.
Anticipate a ground-level contest.
Communicate the spill direction early.

Whether the defender adjusts to the wet football’s flight.
Whether risky marking attempts are reduced.
Whether spoil contact remains firm.
Whether the football is directed away from danger.
Whether landing remains safe.
Whether support players anticipate the spill.

Require two disposals before the defensive exit.

title: Repeat Forward-Entry Defence

coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Create an attacking team and defending team.
Position three feeders around the attacking side of the area with multiple footballs.
Mark two defensive exit gates.
Attackers begin in realistic forward positions.
Defenders match up or organise according to the team’s defensive system.
Feeders deliver consecutive aerial entries with limited delay between possessions.

The first feeder delivers an aerial entry.

The two attackers begin moving to create separate aerial options.

Add full tackling at ground level.

title: Aerial Contest to Boundary Lock
primarySkill: Turning a boundary-side aerial contest into a controlled stoppage.
objective: Develop the defensive unit’s ability to direct a boundary-side aerial contest towards the line and prevent the opposition from escaping into central space.
groundSize: A 25 x 15-metre boundary-side channel.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Mark a boundary line along one side of the channel.
Mark a central escape gate on the opposite side.
Create teams of three attackers and three defenders.
Position one player from each team in the aerial contest.
Place remaining players around the likely ground-ball area.
A feeder delivers down the boundary line.
The defenders attempt to force a boundary or stoppage result.
howTheDrillWorks:
The feeder delivers a high football towards the boundary-side contest.
The aerial defender protects the corridor side and attempts to spoil towards the line.
Ground-level defenders position inside the attacking players.
If the football remains in play, defenders apply controlled pressure and prevent a central release.
The attacking team attempts to move the football through the central escape gate.
The defending team scores for a boundary result, stoppage or possession exit down the line.
The attacking team scores for escaping centrally.
Play continues for a maximum of ten seconds.
Players rotate aerial and ground-level roles after each phase.
coachingPoints: Protect the corridor side of the aerial opponent.
Direct the spoil towards the boundary.
Ground-level defenders should position inside their opponents.
Avoid knocking the football back into central space.
Apply pressure without diving recklessly.
Use the boundary to reduce attacking options.
Communicate whether to gather, tackle or force the ball out.
Accept a stoppage when clean possession is unavailable.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the aerial defender protects the corridor side.
Whether the spoil travels towards the boundary.
Whether ground-level defenders hold inside position.
Whether attackers can escape centrally.
Whether defenders overcommit to the football.

title: Rebound Entry Reorganisation
primarySkill: Reorganising aerial defence after an incomplete defensive clearance.

groundSize: Approximately one-third to one-half of an oval.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback

Create an attacking team and defending team.

Defenders must reorganise while transitioning back towards goal.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team delivers an aerial entry.
Defenders contest and attempt to exit through a gate.
The coach identifies an incomplete or rushed clearance.
A new football is immediately activated from the opposite side.
Defenders turn, scan and rebuild goal-side aerial coverage.
Players communicate new opponents and the primary aerial contestant.
The attacking team attempts to use the disorganised defence.
Defenders attempt to mark, spoil or force the ball towards the boundary.
The sequence ends when the defence controls possession, forces a stoppage or concedes a score.
Teams rotate after three to five sequences.
coachingPoints: React immediately when the exit fails.
Sprint towards defensive shape before searching for a preferred opponent.
Identify the deepest and most dangerous attacker.

title: Pressure and Contest Integration Game

The coach may create temporary attacking numerical advantages.
The attacking team scores for marks or controlled possession inside the central scoring corridor.
The defending team scores for intercept marks, safe spoils, boundary locks, stoppages and controlled exits.

title: Defensive Line Drop-and-Cover

Create an attacking group of four to six players and a defensive group of four to six players.
Position the defenders in a connected line across the field.
Place one or two attackers ahead of the line and additional attackers deeper towards goal.
Position a feeder 30–40 metres from the likely aerial contest.
Mark a deep cover zone behind the primary contest area.
Mark two defensive exit gates towards the boundary.
The feeder may kick to the front of the defensive line or over it into deeper space.

The attacking players begin moving to create short and deep aerial options.
The defensive line scans the feeder and adjusts its collective depth.
As the feeder prepares to kick, the deepest defender communicates whether the line should hold or drop.
When a long kick is delivered, the defender with the strongest line calls and attacks the aerial contest.
The nearest teammate protects the front-and-centre ground ball.
The deepest defender remains behind the contest to protect any football carrying over the back.
If the defenders win possession, they attempt to exit through either boundary gate.
If the attackers win possession, they attempt to score through a central gate.
Play continues for a maximum of twelve seconds.
Teams reset after each completed phase.

title: Weak-Side Aerial Support

Defenders adjust laterally while maintaining goal-side position.
When the ball carrier delivers an aerial entry, the weak-side defender scans the flight and central threat.

Create attacking and defending teams.

The defending team scores by intercepting, spoiling back to support or forcing the ball sideways.

The attacking team begins possession behind the first territory line.
Defenders shift as a connected screen across the middle line.
The attacking team attempts a long aerial kick over or into the screen.
The defender with the strongest line contests the football.
Nearby defenders protect front, central and over-the-back space.
If the defence wins possession, it attempts to move through an exit gate.

Adjust depth according to the ball carrier’s kicking range.
Prevent attackers from standing unopposed behind the screen.

Protect the corridor before wide space.
Direct spoils back towards defensive numbers.
Avoid all midfielders collapsing to the ball.
Re-establish the screen after each possession.

Whether depth reflects the kicker’s range.

title: Post-Spoil Defensive Rotation

Position a key forward and key defender inside the contest area.

commonErrors.correction: Reconnect vision during the forward’s deceleration or turn.

commonErrors.error: Defender grabs after a change of direction.
commonErrors.correction: Recover with foot speed and protect the dangerous shoulder.

commonErrors.error: Technique deteriorates after repeat efforts.
commonErrors.correction: Reduce repetition volume and restore approach control.

progressions: Remove the marked gates.
Add a second mobile forward.
Begin from live forward-half movement.
Vary the feeder’s position.
Add a scoreboard consequence for central marks.
regressions: Limit the forward to two leads.
successIndicators: Recover efficiently to the final lead.
matchApplication: Tall defenders are often targeted by mobile forwards who attempt to create separation through repeated leads. Efficient footwork and space protection allow the defender to retain their aerial advantage without becoming vulnerable on the ground.

title: Defensive 50 Last-Two-Minutes Aerial Scenario
primarySkill: Managing aerial defence while protecting a narrow lead late in a match.
objective: Develop the defensive unit’s ability to select safe aerial outcomes, protect central space and control possession during the final two minutes of a close match.
groundSize: Approximately one-half of an oval including defensive 50 and boundary channels.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Create attacking and defending teams using realistic positional numbers.
Set the defending team four points ahead with two minutes remaining.
Begin with the attacking team in possession outside defensive 50.
Mark boundary-side safety channels and a central scoring corridor.
Position spare footballs with coaches for rapid restarts.
Normal scoring applies.
The defence wins the scenario by preserving the lead until time expires.
howTheDrillWorks:
The clock begins when the attacking team takes possession.
The attack attempts to generate aerial entries and scoring opportunities.
Defenders protect central and goal-side space.
The defender with the strongest line claims each aerial contest.
Disadvantaged defenders spoil towards the boundary or defensive numbers.
If the defence marks, players assess whether to slow play, switch safely or exit down the line.
If the ball reaches ground level, defenders protect the corridor and force a stoppage where appropriate.
Incomplete exits may produce immediate repeat entries.
The scenario ends when time expires or the attacking team takes the lead.
Players review the major aerial and possession decisions before repeating from a different starting point.
coachingPoints: Know the score, time and required result.
Protect the corridor and goal square before low-value wide space.
Use the boundary as a defensive advantage.
Avoid low-percentage intercept attempts from poor position.
Mark when clearly able to secure possession.
Direct spoils away from central crumbers.
Accept a stoppage or controlled minor score when tactically appropriate.
Slow play after winning possession without becoming passive.
Communicate the clock and field position.
Prepare for the repeat entry until the phase is fully controlled.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether defenders understand the scoreboard.
Whether central space remains protected.
Whether aerial risk selection reflects the scenario.
Whether spoil direction reduces scoring danger.
Whether defenders communicate time and roles.
Whether possession is retained after intercept marks.
Whether players force unnecessary corridor exits.
Whether the defence reorganises after incomplete clearances.

commonErrors.error: Defender attempts a high-risk intercept while out of position.
commonErrors.correction: Prioritise preventing the mark and protecting the goal square.

commonErrors.error: Spoil falls centrally to an attacking crumber.
commonErrors.correction: Direct the football towards the boundary or defensive numbers.

commonErrors.error: Players rush possession after an intercept mark.
commonErrors.correction: Assess the clock and use a controlled option.

commonErrors.error: Defenders abandon direct opponents to chase the ball.
commonErrors.correction: Protect dangerous space and maintain role discipline.

commonErrors.error: Team avoids conceding a minor score but gives up a goal.
commonErrors.correction: Select the safest scoreboard outcome.

commonErrors.error: Defenders switch off after the first clearance.
commonErrors.correction: Remain organised until the football leaves the danger area.

progressions: Reduce the defending margin.
Begin with less time remaining.
Start from a boundary throw-in or defensive stoppage.
Add an attacking numerical advantage.
Remove coaching between repeat entries.
regressions: Pause before each entry to organise roles.
Run the scenario without a live scoreboard initially.
successIndicators: Survive repeat entries without losing structure.
matchApplication: Late in close matches, defensive aerial decisions must reflect the scoreboard. The safest result may be a boundary stoppage, a controlled minor score or possession retention rather than an aggressive intercept attempt.
relatedDrills: SP-058 – Aerial Contest to Boundary Lock
SP-060 – Pressure and Contest Integration Game
SP-072 – Deep Forward Match-Up and Goal-Line Support

title: Defending After Kick-In Turnover
primarySkill: Reorganising aerial defence after a turnover from a defensive kick-in.
objective: Develop the defensive unit’s ability to react to a kick-in turnover, recover towards goal and defend the immediate aerial re-entry.
groundSize: Approximately one-half of an oval including the goal square and defensive 50.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Create attacking and defending teams.
Begin each phase with a defensive kick-in.
Position defenders in the team’s normal kick-in structure.
The coach may deliberately activate a turnover at different points of the exit.
Position attacking players to rebound quickly inside 50.
Mark two defensive recovery zones: central goal-side and deep cover.
Spare footballs should be available for rapid re-entry if required.
howTheDrillWorks:
The defence begins a kick-in exit.
Players spread into their normal possession structure.
The coach signals or creates a turnover through an intercepted or incomplete disposal.
The attacking team immediately attempts an aerial re-entry.
Defenders turn, sprint goal side and identify the deepest threats.
Players communicate new match-ups rather than searching only for original opponents.
The defender with the strongest line contests the re-entry.
Supporting defenders protect the front, goal line and likely spoil direction.
If possession is regained, the defence attempts a second controlled exit.
The phase ends after a score, stoppage or completed exit.
Teams rotate after four to six scenarios.
coachingPoints: React immediately to the turnover.
Recover towards goal and dangerous space before locating preferred match-ups.
Identify the deepest opposition target.
Communicate opponent reassignment while running.
Avoid all defenders chasing the ball carrier.
Maintain one player behind or goal side of the aerial contest.
Arrive under control and avoid panic infringements.
Direct the spoil towards boundary-side support.
Prepare the second exit before possession is secured.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Speed of reaction after the turnover.
Whether defenders recover towards goal.
Whether the deepest attacker is identified.
Whether match-ups are communicated.
Whether defenders all move towards the ball carrier.
Whether one player protects behind the contest.
Whether late contact remains legal.
Whether the defence completes the second exit.

commonErrors.error: Defenders hesitate after the turnover.
commonErrors.correction: Turn immediately and sprint towards defensive shape.

commonErrors.error: Players search for original opponents.
commonErrors.correction: Take the nearest dangerous opponent and communicate.

commonErrors.error: All defenders recover towards the ball.
commonErrors.correction: Protect goal-side, deep and central spaces first.

commonErrors.error: Defender arrives late and pushes in the back.
commonErrors.correction: Approach beside the opponent or apply ground-level pressure.

commonErrors.error: Spoil returns to the central corridor.
commonErrors.correction: Direct the football towards the boundary or recovering teammates.

commonErrors.error: Second exit is rushed.
commonErrors.correction: Secure possession and rebuild support before disposing.

progressions: Vary the turnover point.
Add a second rebound entry after an incomplete clearance.
Introduce scoreboard and time pressure.
Remove the coach’s turnover signal and use fully live play.
Expand into full-ground transition.
regressions: Allow defenders several seconds to reorganise.
Stop after the immediate aerial contest.
successIndicators: Identify and communicate the deepest threat.
matchApplication: Kick-in structures spread defenders across the ground and can leave defensive 50 exposed after a turnover. Immediate goal-side recovery and aerial role clarity are required to prevent a rapid opposition score.
relatedDrills: SP-060 – Pressure and Contest Integration Game
SP-072 – Deep Forward Match-Up and Goal-Line Support

title: Final-Quarter Repeat Entry Simulation
primarySkill: Sustaining team aerial defence through repeated final-quarter entries.
objective: Develop the defensive unit’s ability to maintain aerial technique, role discipline and structural connection during repeated high-pressure entries late in a match.
groundSize: Approximately one-half of an oval including defensive 50.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Create attacking and defending teams using realistic positional structures.
Set the scenario in the final quarter with the defending team under sustained pressure.
Position three feeders or attacking restart points around the forward half.
Mark boundary-side defensive exit gates.
The coach activates a new football after incomplete clearances.
Work periods should remain within safe match-like limits.
Provide full recovery and review between scenario blocks.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team begins with an aerial entry.
Defenders organise the aerial contestant and ground-level coverage.
If the defence fails to complete a controlled exit, another entry begins immediately.
Entry location, height and target vary each time.
Defenders must recover shape while fatigued.
One defender attacks the football while teammates protect front, back and weak-side space.
The defence attempts to complete a two-disposal exit through a boundary gate.
The attack attempts to score or retain the football inside 50.
Each block lasts 45–75 seconds depending on the playing group.
Coaches score aerial role clarity, legal technique, ground-level support and exit quality.
Teams rotate after three to five blocks.
coachingPoints: Rebuild defensive shape while the next entry is developing.
Communicate roles despite fatigue and crowd noise.
Preserve one aerial contestant and organised ground coverage.
Control the final approach rather than crashing into contests.
Select the safe spoil direction before take-off.
Maintain a defender goal side or behind the contest.
Avoid rushed central exits.
Use clear leadership to organise tired players.
Stop the block if contact or landing technique becomes unsafe.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether defenders rebuild shape between entries.
Whether communication deteriorates.
Whether multiple players fly as fatigue increases.
Whether final approaches remain controlled.
Whether the deepest space is protected.
Whether spoil direction remains tactical.
Whether ground-level roles remain clear.
Whether exits become rushed.
Whether leaders organise the group.
Whether safe technique is preserved.

commonErrors.error: Defenders watch the previous contest.
commonErrors.correction: Locate the next entry point immediately.

commonErrors.error: Fatigue causes multiple defenders to fly.
commonErrors.correction: Re-establish one-up and supporting-ground roles.

commonErrors.error: Defender enters the contest uncontrolled.
commonErrors.correction: Shorten the final steps and restore balance.

commonErrors.error: Deep cover disappears.
commonErrors.correction: Nominate a player to remain goal side.

commonErrors.error: Spoils return to opposition numbers.
commonErrors.correction: Identify the safe side during the kick’s flight.

commonErrors.error: Defensive exit is forced through the corridor.
commonErrors.correction: Use boundary width and secure the first possession.

commonErrors.error: Communication becomes emotional and unclear.
commonErrors.correction: Use short, agreed team calls.

commonErrors.error: Work periods become unsafe.
commonErrors.correction: Stop the block and increase recovery.

progressions: Reduce recovery between blocks.
Add scoreboard and clock consequences.
Remove fixed feeder positions.
Use fully live repeat entries after turnovers.
Expand into a full-ground final-quarter simulation.
regressions: Limit each block to two entries.
successIndicators: Protect front, back and central space.
matchApplication: Final-quarter defensive periods often include repeat inside-50 entries with limited recovery. Strong teams preserve aerial role discipline and decision quality rather than allowing fatigue to create free kicks, poor spoils or structural collapse.

title: Position-Group Aerial Defence Assessment
primarySkill: Assessing aerial-defence performance according to positional role.
objective: Assess whether defenders can apply the aerial techniques, decisions and team responsibilities required by their specific match role.
groundSize: Approximately one-half of an oval divided into four position-specific assessment stations.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Station 1 assesses key defenders against leading and body-on-body forwards.
Station 2 assesses small defenders managing height mismatches and ground-level recovery.
Station 3 assesses intercept defenders releasing, covering and transitioning.
Station 4 assesses deep defenders coordinating goal-line and repeat-entry defence.
Allocate players according to normal or projected match roles.
Assign a coach or experienced observer to each station.
Use consistent scoring for positioning, judgement, legality, execution, communication and recovery.
Rotate players through secondary roles where appropriate.
howTheDrillWorks:
Players begin at their primary positional station.
Each player completes four to six assessed repetitions.
Key defenders manage varied one-on-one forward movements and deliveries.
Small defenders contest taller targets and must prevent clean marks or win the spill.
Intercept defenders decide when to release and how to cover behind the movement.
Deep defenders organise aerial and goal-line responsibilities.
Each station includes a ground-level continuation or defensive exit.
Coaches record scores and one priority correction.
Players repeat the task after feedback.
Selected players rotate to a secondary positional station.
The assessment concludes with individual and line-level development priorities.
coachingPoints: Assess players against the requirements of their position.
Reward correct decisions, not only successful outcomes.
Observe starting position before the kick.
Assess legal bodywork and approach safety.
Evaluate mark-or-spoil selection.
Judge whether spoil direction assists teammates.
Require communication in all support roles.
Assess ground-level recovery.
Assess whether defensive wins connect to an exit.
Identify transferable skills and role-specific limitations.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Starting position for the assigned role.
Opponent and football awareness.
Movement into the contest.
Legality of contact.
Jump and spoil timing.
Mark-or-spoil decision quality.
Spoil direction.
Communication.
Ground-level recovery.
Team support.
Exit connection.
Consistency across repetitions.

commonErrors.error: Every defender uses the same method regardless of role.
commonErrors.correction: Apply the positioning and decision priorities of the assigned position.

commonErrors.error: Player focuses only on winning the aerial football.
commonErrors.correction: Assess space protection, communication and the next possession.

commonErrors.error: Defender makes technically sound contact but directs it dangerously.
commonErrors.correction: Select a tactical spoil side before take-off.

commonErrors.error: Intercept defender releases without coverage.
commonErrors.correction: Communicate and confirm the rotation behind the movement.

commonErrors.error: Small defender relies only on jumping.
commonErrors.correction: Win position early and compete strongly at ground level.

commonErrors.error: Deep defender leaves the goal line unprotected.
commonErrors.correction: Balance aerial support with last-line responsibility.

progressions: Assess players against unfamiliar opponent types.
Remove station restrictions and use live positional play.
Add scoreboard and time pressure.
Include repeated entries at every station.
Compare results across multiple training blocks.
regressions: Assess technical and tactical components separately.
successIndicators: Connect defensive wins to team possession.
Demonstrate clear positional strengths and development needs.
matchApplication: Different defensive positions require different aerial priorities. Key defenders manage direct opponents, small defenders minimise mismatches, intercept defenders leave opponents to influence passing lanes and deep defenders protect the scoring line and organise support.
relatedDrills: SP-053 – Intercept Defender Versus Leading Lane
SP-072 – Deep Forward Match-Up and Goal-Line Support
SP-074 – Small Defender Aerial Mismatch Management
SP-075 – Tall Defender Versus Mobile Forward

title: Spoiling and Aerial Defence Chapter Final Assessment
primarySkill: Assessing complete spoiling and aerial-defence performance.
objective: Complete a comprehensive assessment of each player’s technical, tactical, positional and team-based aerial-defence capability across realistic Australian football situations.
groundSize: Approximately one-half to two-thirds of an oval, including defensive 50, boundary channels, corridor and goal square.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Divide the assessment into five connected phases.
Phase 1 assesses individual starting position, approach, timing and spoil technique.
Phase 2 assesses live one-on-one contests from front, side and rear positions.
Phase 3 assesses two- and three-defender communication, aerial support and ground-level coverage.
Phase 4 assesses team structure against boundary, corridor, switch and deep entries.
Phase 5 assesses late-match repeat-entry defence and controlled exits.
Allocate players to appropriate positional roles.
Assign coaches to technical, tactical and structural observation responsibilities.
Use a consistent five-point assessment scale for each behaviour.
Modify jumping volume, contact and work duration for age, injury status and masters players.
Prepare emergency and safety procedures before beginning match-like phases.
howTheDrillWorks:
Players complete individual technique repetitions covering approach, jump timing, fist contact, arm selection and landing.
Players enter live one-on-one contests against varied opponent types.
Defenders are assessed on intercept, spoil and safe knockdown decisions.
Small groups complete aerial contests requiring one player to fly and others to protect the ground.
The assessment expands into team entries from the boundary, corridor and weak side.
Coaches activate high, short, floating and deep footballs.
Defenders must communicate roles, direct spoils and reorganise after the contest.
The team then completes a late-match scenario involving repeat entries and scoreboard pressure.
Defensive possession must be connected to a controlled exit.
Coaches record individual and unit-level scores throughout.
Players receive one final assessed repetition after targeted feedback.
The chapter assessment concludes only when every player has completed all required phases safely.
coachingPoints: Assess the complete sequence from starting position to the next possession.
Reward early positioning and flight judgement.
Require legal bodywork and safe approach angles.
Evaluate fist formation, wrist alignment, arm selection and contact point.
Assess whether players mark, spoil or delay according to position and pressure.
Judge spoil direction according to field position and teammate support.
Require an immediate second effort.
Assess communication before, during and after the contest.
Observe whether one defender flies and others protect the ground.
Assess line depth, weak-side support and central protection.
Require organised defensive exits.
Monitor technique and safety under fatigue.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Balanced starting position.
Goal-side and corridor-side protection.
Vision of football and opponent.
Approach speed and final-step control.
Jump timing.
Safe fist and wrist position.
Near-arm and far-arm selection.
Legal body contact.
Mark-or-spoil decision quality.
Direction and distance of the spoil.
Landing control.
Ground-level second effort.
Communication.
Front-and-centre coverage.
Deep and weak-side support.
Match-up transfer.
Repeat-entry organisation.
Scoreboard awareness.
Defensive exit quality.
Consistency under fatigue.

commonErrors.error: Defender focuses only on punching the football.
commonErrors.correction: Assess and coach positioning, decision making, direction and recovery as one sequence.

commonErrors.error: Player approaches too quickly and infringes.
commonErrors.correction: Close space early, then shorten the final steps.

commonErrors.error: Defender watches only the opponent.
commonErrors.correction: Track the football while using peripheral and body awareness.

commonErrors.error: Player uses the preferred arm in every situation.
commonErrors.correction: Select the arm nearest the football and safe spoil side.

commonErrors.error: Defender attempts an intercept from a clear disadvantage.
commonErrors.correction: Prioritise preventing the mark and protecting dangerous space.

commonErrors.error: Spoil creates a second scoring opportunity.
commonErrors.correction: Direct the football towards the boundary, support or maximum safe distance.

commonErrors.error: Multiple defenders fly.
commonErrors.correction: Establish one aerial contestant and maintain ground-level coverage.

commonErrors.error: Defender stops after the spoil.
commonErrors.correction: Land, locate the football and complete the next action.

commonErrors.error: Team structure collapses around the contest.
commonErrors.correction: Retain front, deep, central and weak-side coverage.

commonErrors.error: Defensive possession is turned over immediately.
commonErrors.correction: Secure the first possession and use a supported exit.

commonErrors.error: Fatigue causes unsafe contact or landing.
commonErrors.correction: Stop the repetition, extend recovery and restore technical control.

progressions: Conduct the assessment without marked zones or predetermined entry points.
Use fully live attacking transition.
Add changing scoreboard and time scenarios.
Require defenders to operate in primary and secondary positions.
Compare scores with earlier chapter assessments.
Repeat the assessment during the season to measure retention and improvement.
regressions: Separate technical, contested and tactical phases across multiple sessions.
Use predictable hand-thrown or short-kick deliveries.
Assess younger players using foundation-level stations only.
successIndicators: Execute technically sound spoils with either arm.
Protect central, deep and weak-side space.
Connect defensive wins to controlled exits.
Maintain safe performance under pressure and fatigue.
matchApplication: The assessment reflects the full range of aerial-defence demands in Australian football. Players must defend direct opponents, support teammates, protect dangerous space, make risk-sensitive decisions, direct the football tactically and remain involved until the defensive team controls possession or safely ends the phase.
relatedDrills: SP-060 – Pressure and Contest Integration Game
